nodes.label: L00 - Introduction
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Course introduction lecture: structure, tooling choices, hardware requirements and exam format.

nodes.label: Course Structure
nodes.rationale: The course is split into basic 3D graphics, Vulkan, and shaders/real-time rendering, with theory paired to worked examples.

nodes.label: Vulkan
nodes.rationale: Low-level graphics API used throughout the course; chosen because it is the most widely supported standard for low-level graphics operations across Android, Linux, Windows and (via MoltenVK) iOS/macOS.

nodes.label: C++ as the Host Language
nodes.rationale: C++ interfaces with Vulkan, but only basic features are required so that less technical students can extend pre-built starting points.

nodes.label: Hardware Requirements
nodes.rationale: Vulkan needs a suitable GPU; any full-fledged PC less than 12 years old should work.

nodes.label: Steep Learning Curve of CG Applications
nodes.rationale: CG development shows nothing on screen for a long stretch, which is why examples exist: to give visual feedback in stages where none would otherwise be possible.
nodes.norm_label: steep learning curve of cg applications

nodes.label: Exam: Project and Oral Discussion
nodes.rationale: The exam is a project presented with an oral discussion plus possible theory questions; topics are released after mid-course.

nodes.label: Application Fields of Computer Graphics
nodes.rationale: Video game design, scientific visualization and architectural visualization are the cited target domains.

nodes.label: L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on how graphics hardware stores pixels, how colour is encoded and reproduced, and the 2D primitives and coordinate systems used to draw.
nodes.norm_label: l01 - graphics adapters, colors and 2d drawings

nodes.label: Pixel
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: A picture element: one individually assignable cell of the rectangular matrix the adapter divides the screen into.

nodes.label: Raster Graphics
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Images represented as a grid of coloured pixels obtained by spatial sampling, as opposed to vector descriptions.

nodes.label: Video Memory (VRAM)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Dedicated memory on the graphics card holding the frame buffer plus other images and data read by the GPU.

nodes.label: Frame Buffer (Screen Buffer)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: The region of VRAM encoding the colour of every pixel currently displayed, read out by the RAMDAC/display controller.

nodes.label: GPU Command List
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Modern applications never write the screen buffer directly; they submit a list of drawing, text, blit and projection commands that the GPU executes to compose the image.

nodes.label: Driver and Library Abstraction of the Adapter
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Adapters are co-designed with their drivers, so the programmer never touches registers or GPU directly; Vulkan unifies access across the huge variety of cards, which is also why environment setup is so hard.
nodes.norm_label: driver and library abstraction of the adapter

nodes.label: RGB Colour Coding
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: On-screen colours are encoded as red, green and blue levels, mirroring the three cone types of the human eye.

nodes.label: Human Colour Vision (Rods and Cones)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Rods sense intensity while three cone types sense different portions of the spectrum, and the brain combines their stimuli into a perceived colour.

nodes.label: Colour Reproduction and Additive Mixing
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Displays invert the vision process by emitting the three primaries, which the eye mixes at distance into yellow, cyan, magenta or white.

nodes.label: Colour Range (Gamut)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: A monitor reproduces only a triangular subset of the parabolic spectrum the eye can see, and its reproducible colours form an RGB cube.

nodes.label: Colour Quantization
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Because the RGB levels are digital and pass through a DAC, they are quantized, further reducing the number of displayable colours.

nodes.label: Colour Profiles
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Compensation data that makes different monitors, which emit slightly different primaries, behave uniformly; out of scope for the course.

nodes.label: Image and Display Resolution
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Pixel density (DPI) for images, and the horizontal Sw by vertical Sh pixel counts for screens.

nodes.label: Pixel Aspect Ratio
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Pixels are not necessarily square, so horizontal and vertical resolutions can differ in metric terms.

nodes.label: 2D Graphics Primitives
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Current adapters draw everything from just three primitives - points, lines and filled triangles - which is why the theory reduces to these.

nodes.label: Point Primitive (plot)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: The simplest primitive: plot() sets the colour of a single pixel at given coordinates.

nodes.label: Line Primitive
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Connects two given endpoints with a straight coloured segment; used to draw empty (non-filled) objects.

nodes.label: Filled Triangle Primitive
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Specified by three vertices and a colour; filled triangles are the basis of all 3D computer graphics.

nodes.label: Pixel (Device) Coordinates
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Left-handed integer Cartesian system with the origin at the top-left, x growing right and y growing down, ranging 0..sw-1 and 0..sh-1.

nodes.label: Clipping
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Cutting primitives so only their visible fraction is drawn; without it the primitive may wrap around or write unallocated memory.

nodes.label: Normalized Screen Coordinates
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Device, size and shape independent Cartesian coordinates (in Vulkan [-1,1] with y pointing down, in OpenGL y up) that let one program address any surface regardless of resolution.

nodes.label: Surface (Render Target)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L01 - Graphics Adapters, Colors and 2D Drawings.txt
nodes.rationale: Generic term covering every output scenario - full screen, resizable window, or an arbitrary memory area rendered to.

nodes.label: L02 - 3D coordinates and transforms
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture introducing homogeneous coordinates and the 4x4 matrix encoding of affine transforms, their inversion and composition.

nodes.label: Homogeneous Coordinates
nodes.rationale: A 3D point written with four values x,y,z,w where w is a scale factor; all linearly dependent tuples denote the same point, and dividing by w recovers Cartesian coordinates.

nodes.label: Affine Transforms
nodes.rationale: The large family of transformations - translation, scaling, rotation, shear - applied identically to every point of an object.

nodes.label: 4x4 Matrix Transforms
nodes.rationale: Affine transforms encode as 4x4 matrices acting on homogeneous points; the last row |0 0 0 1| keeps w unchanged, the upper 3x3 block holds rotation/scale/shear and the last column the translation.

nodes.label: Matrix-on-the-Left Convention
nodes.rationale: The course multiplies column vectors on the right of the matrix because that is the textbook convention; Vulkan supports either, but many helper libraries use matrix-on-the-right with transposed matrices, so knowing which one is in use matters.

nodes.label: Identity Transform
nodes.rationale: The 4x4 identity matrix, which leaves every point unchanged.

nodes.label: Translation
nodes.rationale: Moves every point by dx,dy,dz while preserving size and orientation; built by placing the offsets in the last column of the identity.

nodes.label: Scaling
nodes.rationale: Changes size around a centre by multiplying coordinates with factors placed on the matrix diagonal; proportional when all factors are equal.

nodes.label: Mirroring (Planar, Axial, Central)
nodes.rationale: Symmetry obtained with negative scaling factors: one negative factor mirrors about a plane, two about an axis, three about the origin.

nodes.label: Flattening (Zero Scale Factor)
nodes.rationale: A scaling factor of 0 collapses the object along an axis, losing one dimension, which is also why such a transform cannot be inverted.

nodes.label: Rotation
nodes.rationale: Changes orientation about an axis whose points stay fixed; Rx, Ry and Rz encode rotations about the three reference axes through the origin.

nodes.label: Shear
nodes.rationale: Bends an object linearly along an axis by two shear factors, expressed with matrices Hx, Hy, Hz.

nodes.label: Transform Matrix as New Axes and Origin
nodes.rationale: The columns of the 3x3 block are the directions and lengths of the new axes in the old system and the last column is the new origin, which makes it easy to define a transform by naming its centre and axes.
nodes.norm_label: transform matrix as new axes and origin

nodes.label: Inversion of Transformations
nodes.rationale: Undoing a transform means inverting its matrix; simple patterns exist (negated translation, reciprocal scaling, negated rotation angle) and inversion fails only when an axis degenerates, two axes align, or one lies in the plane of the others.

nodes.label: Composition of Transformations
nodes.rationale: Chaining transforms as a matrix product; associativity lets all of them be factorized into a single matrix applied once per vertex, which is why composition is cheap.

nodes.label: Non-Commutativity of Transform Order
nodes.rationale: Matrix product is not commutative, so swapping two transformations changes the result; matrices also appear in the expression in reverse order with respect to the transformations they represent.

nodes.label: L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on transforms about arbitrary axes and centres, and on parallel (orthogonal) projections from world coordinates to 3D normalized screen coordinates.
nodes.norm_label: l03 - advanced transforms and parallel projections

nodes.label: Transformations Around an Arbitrary Axis or Centre
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Any rotation, scaling, shear or symmetry about an arbitrary axis is built by translating the centre to the origin, aligning a main axis with elementary rotations, applying the transform and undoing the alignment.
nodes.norm_label: transformations around an arbitrary axis or centre

nodes.label: Inverse of a Composed Transform
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: The inverse of a product is the product of the inverses in reverse order, so a chain of transforms can be inverted without any numerical matrix inversion.

nodes.label: Axis-Angle Rotation Matrix
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Closed-form rotation matrix for an angle about a unit vector n, avoiding the five-transform decomposition; derivation is out of scope and left to an external reference.

nodes.label: Projection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Constructing a 2D image of a 3D scene as the intersection of projection rays with a projection surface; studied since Duerer in the XVI century.

nodes.label: Planar Projection and Projection Plane
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: The course only considers planar projections because straight 3D segments stay straight on screen, so projecting the vertices and reconnecting them suffices; on spherical VR surfaces lines become curves.

nodes.label: Parallel vs Perspective Projection Types
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Parallel projections keep apparent size independent of distance (technical drawings) while perspective rays converge on a centre of projection (immersive views).

nodes.label: World Coordinates (y-up, right-handed)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Global Cartesian system describing the scene; the course uses y-up right-handed with z out of the screen, while tools like Blender use z-up, so awareness of the convention is what matters.

nodes.label: 3D Normalized Screen Coordinates
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Normalized screen coordinates plus a depth component (in Vulkan in [0,1], smaller z closer to the viewer) needed to sort faces correctly; OpenGL uses a different range.

nodes.label: Orthogonal Projection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Parallel projection whose plane is one of the xy, yz or zx planes with rays perpendicular to it, so equal-length segments parallel to an axis stay equal regardless of distance.

nodes.label: Near and Far Planes
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Depth limits of the visible volume, needed to avoid drawing objects behind the observer or too far away and to confine the normalized z to the 0..1 range.

nodes.label: Orthogonal Projection Matrix (Port)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Built in three composed steps - a translation bringing the box centre at the near plane to the origin, a non-uniform scaling into the canonical ranges, and a mirror fixing the Vulkan y and z directions.

nodes.label: Aspect Ratio in Projection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Since normalized screen coordinates ignore the physical proportions of the display, the projection matrix must make r-l equal to a times t-b to avoid distortion; a centred box then needs only half-width w, n, f and a.

nodes.label: No Perspective Divide for Parallel Projections
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L03 - Advanced Transforms and Parallel Projections.txt
nodes.rationale: Because parallel projections are conventional transform matrices with last row |0 0 0 1|, w stays 1 and the fourth component can simply be discarded instead of dividing.
nodes.norm_label: no perspective divide for parallel projections

nodes.label: L04 - Axonometric and Perspective Projections
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture covering axonometric and oblique parallel projections and the full derivation of the perspective projection matrix with camera parameters.

nodes.label: Axonometric Projection
nodes.rationale: Parallel projection that shows all faces of a box-shaped object at once, fixing the loss of depth perception when a cube aligned to the axes projects to a square.

nodes.label: Orthographic Projection
nodes.rationale: The subset of axonometric projections whose rays stay perpendicular to the rotated projection plane.

nodes.label: Isometric, Dimetric and Trimetric Projections
nodes.rationale: The three main families of axonometric projections, differing in how many axes share the same foreshortening.

nodes.label: Oblique Projection
nodes.rationale: Parallel rays oblique to the plane, keeping x and y parallel to the screen while z is angled; implemented by pre-multiplying an extra transform matrix before the parallel projection.

nodes.label: Perspective Projection
nodes.rationale: Rays converging on a projection centre produce magnification with distance; the screen coordinates follow from the similar triangles relation xs = d*x/-z, ys = d*y/-z.

nodes.label: Projection Distance d as Focal Length
nodes.rationale: The centre-to-plane distance d behaves like a camera focal length: small d is a wide lens exaggerating depth and capturing more objects, large d a tele lens flattening depth, and d to infinity degenerates into a parallel projection.
nodes.norm_label: projection distance d as focal length

nodes.label: Perspective Projection Matrix (Ppersp)
nodes.rationale: A 4x4 matrix whose last row is not |0 0 0 1|, so the result has w different from 1 and the perspective divide performs the division by -z; a 1 added in the third row keeps a monotonic depth value.

nodes.label: Perspective Divide (w Division)
nodes.rationale: Dividing the transformed homogeneous vector by its w component is what turns the linear matrix product into the non-linear perspective foreshortening.

nodes.label: View Frustum
nodes.rationale: The visible volume in perspective is a truncated pyramid rather than a box, since the screen borders widen from the near to the far plane; asymmetric borders allow shifted viewports spanning several screens.

nodes.label: Field of View and Camera Parameters
nodes.rationale: Rather than l, r, t, b the matrix is usually parameterized like a camera by near and far distances, the vertical fov-y angle and the aspect ratio, with t = n*tan(fov/2).
nodes.norm_label: field of view and camera parameters

nodes.label: L05 - View and World Matrices
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture deriving the camera and view matrices (look-in-direction and look-at) and the world matrix from Euler angles or quaternions.

nodes.label: Compass Convention for Directions
nodes.rationale: Teaching convention placing North on the negative z-axis and East on the positive x-axis to describe orientations in the y-up world.

nodes.label: Camera Matrix (Mc)
nodes.rationale: Transform that moves a camera - modelled as an object at the origin looking down the negative z-axis - to its target position and orientation.

nodes.label: View Matrix (Mv)
nodes.rationale: The inverse of the camera matrix; applying it to the whole scene rebuilds a world in which the projection plane sits exactly where the fixed projection matrices assume it.

nodes.label: View-Projection Matrix (Mvp)
nodes.rationale: Projection matrix times view matrix, taking a point from world homogeneous coordinates to 3D normalized screen coordinates as seen by the camera.

nodes.label: Look-in-Direction Camera Model
nodes.rationale: First-person model where the camera is given by its position plus direction (yaw), elevation (pitch) and roll angles, composed as T*Ry*Rx*Rz and then inverted.

nodes.label: Look-At Camera Model
nodes.rationale: Third-person model where the camera at c aims at a target a with an up vector u; the axes vz, vx, vy are built by normalization and cross products and placed in the camera matrix columns.

nodes.label: Up Vector
nodes.rationale: Direction perpendicular to the ground, usually (0,1,0) in y-up systems, that fixes the remaining rotational degree of freedom of a look-at camera; games such as Super Mario Galaxy vary it deliberately.

nodes.label: Cross Product and Degenerate Up Vector
nodes.rationale: The normalized cross product yields the camera x-axis, but returns zero when the view direction aligns with the up vector, in which case the previous matrix or a random x-axis must be reused.
nodes.norm_label: cross product and degenerate up vector

nodes.label: Fast Inversion of an Orthonormal Camera Matrix
nodes.rationale: Because the look-at axes are orthonormal, the view matrix is obtained with a transposition and one matrix-vector product instead of a general inversion.
nodes.norm_label: fast inversion of an orthonormal camera matrix

nodes.label: Local (Model) Coordinates
nodes.rationale: The coordinates of an object's points as authored in the modelling tool, before being placed in the scene.

nodes.label: World Matrix (Mw)
nodes.rationale: Transforms local coordinates into world coordinates as T * Ry(yaw) * Rx(pitch) * Rz(roll) * S: scaling first so directions are not skewed, translation last so the position is independent of size and orientation.

nodes.label: Asset Origin and Facing Convention
nodes.rationale: Models must be authored with the origin at the most representative point and a defined facing axis, an extra skill for artists working on interactive 3D rather than animation.

nodes.label: Euler Angles (Roll, Pitch, Yaw)
nodes.rationale: Three intuitive angles defining an orientation, always applied in roll-pitch-yaw order, which maps to the z, x, y axis order in a y-up system facing positive z.

nodes.label: Adaptation Matrix (Ma)
nodes.rationale: Extra matrix chained before the world matrix to reconcile third-party assets authored with a different up axis, scale or origin with the project conventions; it cannot be generalized and must be custom per asset.

nodes.label: Gimbal Lock
nodes.rationale: When pitch reaches 90 degrees the roll and yaw axes superimpose and a degree of freedom is lost, which breaks Euler angles for flight or space simulators though not for planar games.

nodes.label: Quaternion
nodes.rationale: Extension of complex numbers with three imaginary components i, j, k satisfying i2=j2=k2=ijk=-1, with its own sum, product, norm, power and phase algebra.

nodes.label: Quaternion Rotation
nodes.rationale: A unit quaternion cos(t/2)+sin(t/2)(ix+jy+kz) encodes a rotation of angle t about a unit axis, converts directly to a rotation matrix, and composes by non-commutative product - the standard cure for gimbal lock.

nodes.label: L06 - Depth testing and Meshes
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture covering how 3D surfaces are encoded as polygonal meshes and how visibility between overlapping primitives is resolved with the z-buffer and stencil buffer.

nodes.label: Mesh
nodes.rationale: A set of adjacent triangles that approximates the boundary surface of a solid object; all other surface models are converted to meshes before display.

nodes.label: Face
nodes.rationale: A polygon describing a planar portion of the surface of an object.

nodes.label: Edge
nodes.rationale: The side of a polygon, normally corresponding to the intersection of two faces.

nodes.label: Vertex
nodes.rationale: The starting or ending point of an edge; stored in Cartesian coordinates and made homogeneous by the engine before the World-View-Projection transform.

nodes.label: Point Cloud
nodes.rationale: Encoding an object as a bare set of points, rejected because even ~10k points still look empty and it costs too many resources.

nodes.label: Surface Representation Models
nodes.rationale: Computational-geometry alternatives for describing surfaces (meshes, Hermite surfaces, NURBS, hierarchical subdivision surfaces, metaballs), all eventually tessellated to meshes for display.

nodes.label: NURBS
nodes.rationale: Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines, a parametric surface model offered by authoring tools such as Blender.

nodes.label: 2-Manifold Topology
nodes.rationale: A surface where every edge is adjacent to exactly two faces; non-2-manifold meshes (holes, lamina faces) represent non-physical objects and break algorithms such as back-face culling.

nodes.label: Polygon Tessellation
nodes.rationale: Reducing any polygon to a set of triangles, needed because polygons with more than three vertices may not be planar; the subdivision is not unique.

nodes.label: Triangle List
nodes.rationale: Mesh encoding storing three separate vertices per triangle with no reuse, needing 3N vertices for N triangles but able to encode unconnected triangles.

nodes.label: Triangle Strip
nodes.rationale: Mesh encoding of a band of adjacent triangles where each new vertex joins the previous two, needing only N+2 vertices for N triangles.

nodes.label: Triangle Fan
nodes.rationale: An OpenGL-standard encoding made optional in Vulkan, so some adapters may not support it and the course skips it.

nodes.label: Vertex Reuse Constraint
nodes.rationale: A strip or indexed encoding can be used only when the reused vertices are identical in ALL their parameters (position, normal, texture coordinates), not just position.

nodes.label: Indexed Primitives
nodes.rationale: Encoding a mesh with a vertex array plus an index array, so a vertex shared between several strips or triangles is stored only once.

nodes.label: Vertex Array
nodes.rationale: The array holding the actual definitions (positions and other attributes) of the distinct vertices of an indexed primitive.

nodes.label: Index Array
nodes.rationale: The array that defines the triangles by referring to positions in the vertex array; e.g. 36 indices describe the 12 triangles of a cube.

nodes.label: Line List
nodes.rationale: Wireframe encoding storing each segment as two separate vertices, requiring 2N vertices for N segments.

nodes.label: Line Strip
nodes.rationale: Wireframe encoding of a connected path where each vertex joins the previous one, requiring N+1 vertices for N segments.

nodes.label: Point List
nodes.rationale: Vulkan primitive encoding used for particle-like effects where each element is a single position in space.

nodes.label: Wireframe View
nodes.rationale: Rendering only object boundaries with lines, useful for debugging a 3D application and for 2D plots and charts.

nodes.label: Hidden Surfaces Elimination
nodes.rationale: Respecting the proper visualization order of primitives so that nearer polygons cover the ones behind them.

nodes.label: Painter Algorithm
nodes.rationale: Drawing primitives in reverse order of distance from the projection plane; it fails for cyclically overlapping primitives unless they are split.

nodes.label: Z-Buffer (Depth Testing)
nodes.rationale: A per-pixel memory area storing the normalized screen z of the pixel currently displayed; a new fragment is written only if its distance is smaller, which splits primitives at pixel level and removes any need to sort them.

nodes.label: Z-Fighting
nodes.rationale: Artifact where the final color of two almost co-planar surfaces is decided by the round-off of their discretized depths, caused by the non-uniform precision of the z range.

nodes.label: Near and Far Plane Setting
nodes.rationale: Because z is normalized against the near and far planes, they must be chosen appropriately for the scene rather than arbitrarily small and large, otherwise depth precision collapses.

nodes.label: Stencil Buffer
nodes.rationale: A per-pixel integer buffer, often a single bit, used to forbid drawing in some screen regions (HUD, cockpit) or to build shadows, reflections and contours in multi-pass rendering.

nodes.label: Back-Face Culling
nodes.rationale: Discarding faces turned away from the viewer; it does not work on non-2-manifold objects.

nodes.label: L07 - Rendering
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture introducing radiometric quantities, the BRDF and the full rendering equation together with its extensions to transmission and subsurface scattering.

nodes.label: Rendering
nodes.rationale: The process of creating realistic 3D images with accurate colors by emulating how light is reflected between the light sources and the surfaces of the scene.

nodes.label: Energy
nodes.rationale: Total light emitted by a surface in all directions during a time interval, measured in Joules.

nodes.label: Power
nodes.rationale: Instantaneous light energy emitted by a surface in all directions, measured in Watts.

nodes.label: Irradiance
nodes.rationale: Fraction of power emitted by a point of a surface in all directions, denoted E and measured in W/m2; obtained by integrating radiance over the hemisphere.

nodes.label: Radiance
nodes.rationale: Energy emitted at an instant from a point of a surface in each direction, denoted L and measured in W/(m2 sr); the use of solid angles makes it independent of viewing distance, and sensors including the eye respond proportionally to it.

nodes.label: BRDF (Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function)
nodes.rationale: Function of the incoming and outgoing unit directions that tells how much irradiance arriving from one angle is reflected toward another, measured in sr-1 and determined by the microscopic structure of the material.

nodes.label: Reciprocity
nodes.rationale: Property of a good BRDF whereby swapping the ingoing and outgoing directions leaves the value unchanged, which is why the function is called bidirectional.

nodes.label: Energy Conservation
nodes.rationale: Property whereby a BRDF cannot increase the total irradiance leaving a point; the integral over all angles is dimensionless and may be below one if the point absorbs energy.

nodes.label: Normal Vector
nodes.rationale: Vector perpendicular to a surface that identifies its orientation and serves as the reference axis for the BRDF.

nodes.label: Tangent Vector
nodes.rationale: An arbitrary vector lying on the surface and perpendicular to the normal, providing the angular reference needed by the BRDF.

nodes.label: Rendering Equation
nodes.rationale: Relation determining the radiance leaving each point x of a scene in each output direction as the sum of its own emission and the BRDF-weighted integral of the radiance arriving from every other point; since L appears on both sides it is an integral equation of the second kind.

nodes.label: Emission Term Le
nodes.rationale: Term accounting for the light an object emits by itself at point x in direction wr; it characterizes light sources and is how the rendering process is seeded with photons.

nodes.label: Geometric Term G(x,y)
nodes.rationale: Factor encoding the geometric relation between two points through two cosines against the respective normals and the squared distance between them.

nodes.label: Visibility Term V(x,y)
nodes.rationale: Binary term that is 1 when two points can see each other and 0 when occluded; it is what produces shadows and keeps at most one opaque object per input direction.

nodes.label: MERL BRDF Database
nodes.rationale: Cited public database of measured BRDFs.

nodes.label: BTDF (Bidirectional Transmittance Distribution Function)
nodes.rationale: Extension of the BRDF for transmitted light (transparency), defined similarly but oriented on the opposite side of the surface.

nodes.label: BSDF (Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function)
nodes.rationale: Single function merging BRDF and BTDF, possible because their output angles normally do not overlap.

nodes.label: Sub-Surface Scattering
nodes.rationale: Phenomenon where light bounces inside an object and exits from a different point, typical of human skin and marble.

nodes.label: BSSRDF
nodes.rationale: Function with an extra entry-point parameter x' that models subsurface scattering, forcing the rendering equation to integrate over all the points of the object.

nodes.label: Participating Media
nodes.rationale: Gases and fumes, an effect the basic rendering equation cannot simulate, alongside transparent materials such as glass and water.

nodes.label: Per-Wavelength RGB Solution
nodes.rationale: The rendering equation is solved once per wavelength, normally the three RGB channels, while the geometric and visibility terms are wavelength independent and shared.

nodes.label: L08 - Pipelines
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on direct versus indirect lighting, the Vulkan pipeline types and the stages of the graphics pipeline that implement scan-line rendering and ray casting.

nodes.label: Direct Light Sources
nodes.rationale: Lights coming from specific positions and directions such as a lamp, a spotlight or the sun; using them alone makes unlit points pitch black, which is unrealistic but is the basic simplification of real-time CG.

nodes.label: Indirect Light Sources
nodes.rationale: Illumination caused by light bounces and reflections among surfaces; accurate computation is too costly in real time so it is approximated with contributions precomputed off-line and stored in images.

nodes.label: Hard Light
nodes.rationale: A light that produces clearly separated shadows and highlights.

nodes.label: Soft Light
nodes.rationale: A light producing diffuse illumination whose shadows and highlights blend with the surrounding surfaces.

nodes.label: Projected Shadows
nodes.rationale: Shadows created by the occlusion of direct light sources; they are not simple to obtain and are approximated with specific techniques such as shadow maps.

nodes.label: Pipeline
nodes.rationale: A structure where a stream of data is processed through a sequence of steps so that different elements occupy different stages in parallel; stages are either system defined (user configurable) or user programmed.

nodes.label: Shader
nodes.rationale: The name given for historical reasons to the algorithms running in the programmable stages of a pipeline.

nodes.label: Graphics Pipeline
nodes.rationale: The Vulkan pipeline type that implements scan-line rendering, offering up to five shader stages of which only the vertex and fragment ones are mandatory; each distinct set of shaders in an application needs its own pipeline object.

nodes.label: Ray-Tracing Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Vulkan pipeline type for ray-traced rendering of 3D meshes, standardized only recently and therefore with limited support on many systems.

nodes.label: Mesh Shading Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Vulkan pipeline type for mesh rendering that is still in an early stage with limited hardware support.

nodes.label: Compute Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Vulkan pipeline type used for general purpose GPU computation rather than for rendering meshes.

nodes.label: Scan-Line Rendering
nodes.rationale: Simplest approximation of the rendering equation: objects and invisible light sources are kept separate, inter-reflection is dropped so the integral becomes a summation over the direct lights, the geometric term is folded into the BRDF, and visibility is handled only against the observer via the z-buffer, so no projected shadows, reflections or refractions appear.

nodes.label: Ray Casting
nodes.rationale: Extension of scan-line rendering that evaluates the visibility function between each point and each light by casting a ray, thereby adding projected shadows; it is the technique used by most course examples.

nodes.label: Radiosity
nodes.rationale: One of the techniques introduced to approximate the rendering equation, mentioned alongside ray tracing and Montecarlo methods.

nodes.label: Montecarlo Techniques
nodes.rationale: Stochastic approximation methods for the rendering equation, closely tied to the pipeline types that support them.

nodes.label: Vertex Shader
nodes.rationale: Mandatory programmable stage executed once per vertex that multiplies local positions by the WVP matrix to obtain clipping coordinates, computes colors and normals for later stages, and deforms skins.

nodes.label: Fragment Shader
nodes.rationale: Mandatory programmable stage that determines the final color of each fragment, i.e. computes the approximate solution of the rendering equation for that pixel using physically based or artistic models.

nodes.label: Tessellation Shader
nodes.rationale: Optional stage that raises the resolution of an object, e.g. subdividing a sphere more finely when it is close to the viewer; not covered in the course.

nodes.label: Geometry Shader
nodes.rationale: Optional stage that adds or removes primitives from the stream; it could replace tessellation but its generality would mean more complex code and slower performance.

nodes.label: Rasterization
nodes.rationale: Fixed stage that generates the fragments of each primitive line after line from left to right (the origin of the name scan-line) and performs the division by w turning clipping into normalized screen coordinates.

nodes.label: Fragment
nodes.rationale: A candidate contribution to a screen pixel; several fragments can be merged into one pixel, which is why they are not simply called pixels.

nodes.label: Anti-Aliasing
nodes.rationale: Quality technique that merges several fragments into a single screen pixel.

nodes.label: Color Blending
nodes.rationale: Final stage where computed colors either replace or are combined with the ones already in the framebuffer, enabling transparency and other blending effects.

nodes.label: Fixed Functions
nodes.rationale: Non-programmable pipeline sections that perform primitive clipping, back-face culling, depth testing and stencil operations.

nodes.label: Shadow Map
nodes.rationale: Image rendered from the light position storing per-pixel distance to the light; a later pass compares the shader-computed distance against it to decide whether the light reaches the point, giving real-time ray casting through multi-pass rendering.

nodes.label: Starter.hpp Wrapper
nodes.rationale: Wrapper developed at Politecnico that simplifies Vulkan pipeline creation by setting most of the many configurable parameters to meaningful defaults.

nodes.label: L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture defining the three basic direct light models (directional, point, spot) and the diffuse and specular BRDF components used in real-time rendering.
nodes.norm_label: l09 - light models and basic brdfs

nodes.label: Light Model
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Function that, given the position x of a point of an object, returns the direction of the light and the color/intensity received there; each term of the scan-line summation is the product of a light model and a BRDF.

nodes.label: Light Direction lx
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Unit vector that by convention points from the surface point toward the light source.

nodes.label: Light Color
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: RGB vector giving the light intensity per wavelength; components must be non-negative but may exceed 1 to model stronger sources.

nodes.label: Component-Wise vs Dot Product Notation
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Course convention where * denotes the component-wise product of two colors and the dot denotes the scalar product of two geometric vectors, needed because both the light color and the BRDF return RGB vectors.

nodes.label: Directional (Direct) Light
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Model for distant sources such as sunlight: the rays are parallel everywhere, so both the direction vector d and the color l are constants independent of the position x on the object.

nodes.label: Point Light
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Omnidirectional source parameterized by a position p and a color l, used for lamps, bulbs and candles; the direction is the normalized p-x, which varies over the illuminated surface, and the intensity is scaled by a decay factor.

nodes.label: Spot Light
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Conic projector defined by a position p and a unit direction d that confines another light model by modulating its color with a cone dimming term; the popular implementation adds the dimming to a point light, so decay, target distance g and color are inherited.

nodes.label: Decay Factor beta
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: User-selectable exponent making the attenuation constant, inverse-linear or inverse-squared; the physically correct inverse-square law is often abandoned because without indirect lighting it makes CG images too dark, and the angular decay of the reflection already darkens the result.

nodes.label: Target Distance g
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Distance at which the light reduction factor is exactly 1: closer than g the intensity exceeds l, farther it dims; together with beta it lets a shader keep colors in the 0..1 range and tweak the result instead of using true radiance values.

nodes.label: Inner and Outer Cone Angles
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: The two angles aIN and aOUT that split the spotlight cone into a constant zone, a linearly decaying zone and an absent zone; implementations use the cosines of the half-angles cIN and cOUT, with cIN greater than cOUT.

nodes.label: Cone Dimming Term
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Clamped ratio built from the dot product between the light direction and the spot axis minus cOUT, divided by cIN minus cOUT, producing the smooth transition between the intense and dark zones of a spotlight.

nodes.label: Cosine Light Model
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Degenerate spotlight where the inner cone shrinks to zero and the outer cosine reaches one, leaving only a clamped cosine factor; very simple yet it produces interesting diffuse lighting effects.

nodes.label: Area Light
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Model capturing the actual shape of a real source; because the whole light shape must be integrated, the summation becomes an integral even in scan-line rendering and the solution cannot be decoupled from the surface BRDF.

nodes.label: Diffuse Reflection Component
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: The part of the BRDF that represents the main color of the object; real-time BRDFs are written as the sum of a diffuse and a specular term and usually give up energy conservation for artistic and efficiency reasons.

nodes.label: Specular Reflection Component
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: The part of the BRDF accounting for light reflected near the mirror direction; the rougher the surface the wider the spread and the larger the highlight, and the number and shape of the highlights match the direct light sources in the scene.

nodes.label: Mirror Reflection Direction
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Direction r = 2(d.nx)nx - d obtained by projecting the light vector onto the normal and reflecting it; GLSL offers a built-in reflect() function that computes it with the opposite sign convention.

nodes.label: Lambert Diffuse Reflection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Simplest BRDF, a constant equal to the diffuse color mD scaled by max(0, cos of the angle between the surface normal nx and the light direction d); the reflection is independent of the viewing angle and the clamp prevents back faces from subtracting light.

nodes.label: Diffuse Color mD
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: RGB vector expressing the material's ability to reflect each primary frequency by Lambert diffusion; it is specified as a color because a perfectly white perpendicular light returns exactly mD, and it is the base color of the surface.

nodes.label: Specular Color mS
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: RGB vector defining how the incoming light is reflected in the specular lobe; it is white for most objects so highlights take the light color, while metals such as gold or copper set mS equal to mD.

nodes.label: Specular Power gamma
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Exponent applied to the specular cosine: the greater it is the smaller the highlight and the shinier the surface, with practical values often in the order of one or two hundred.

nodes.label: Phong Specular Reflection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Specular model that first builds the mirror direction r and then raises the clamped cosine of the angle between r and the observer direction to the specular power.

nodes.label: Blinn Specular Reflection
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Alternative specular model that raises the clamped dot product between the normal and the half vector to the specular power; slightly more expensive than Phong because of the normalization, and it yields a wider decay area, so artists usually keep both.

nodes.label: Half Vector h
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Normalized average of the light direction and the viewer direction; the angle between the normal and h approximates the angle between the observer and the reflected ray.

nodes.label: Oren-Nayar Diffuse Model
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Diffuse reflection model listed after Lambert in order of implementation complexity.

nodes.label: Toon Shading
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Non-photorealistic model presented in the course as both a diffuse and a specular reflection variant.

nodes.label: Ward Specular Model
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Anisotropic specular reflection model listed among those covered by the course.

nodes.label: Cook-Torrance Specular Model
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Microfacet-based specular reflection model, the most complex of the specular models listed in the course.

nodes.label: Color Clamping
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Clamping the summed pixel color back into [0,1] at the end of the computation; Vulkan does it automatically on the fragment shader output but explicit clamping is preferable, and the effect resembles photographic overexposure.

nodes.label: High Dynamic Range (HDR)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Technique that computes colors outside [0,1] and maps them back with a non-linear tone function based on luminance, preserving detail in both dark and very lit areas at the cost of four times the memory and extra computation.

nodes.label: Simplified BRDF Parameterization
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L09 - Light Models and basic BRDFs.txt
nodes.rationale: Since nearly all diffuse and specular models depend only on the light direction, the normal, the view direction and a few model-specific parameters, they can be written uniformly as fD(d,n,v,pD) and fS(d,n,v,pS).

nodes.label: L10 - Smooth shading
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on how per-vertex data is interpolated toward the fragment shader and how per-vertex normal vectors let a faceted mesh look smooth.

nodes.label: Vertex-Fragment Shader Connection
nodes.rationale: Besides the normalized screen coordinates, the vertex shader emits any extra data the fragment shader needs to solve the rendering equation, and the fixed part of the pipeline interpolates all of it automatically.

nodes.label: World Space Coordinates xW
nodes.rationale: Vertex position multiplied only by the World matrix; it must be passed to the fragment shader because the point and spot light directions and the perspective viewer direction all need the world-space position of the shaded point.

nodes.label: Barycentric Coordinates
nodes.rationale: The three coefficients a1, a2, a3 of the convex linear combination that expresses an internal point of a triangle from its vertices, found by solving a linear system.

nodes.label: Barycentric Interpolation
nodes.rationale: Applying the barycentric coefficients of a point to the values attached to the three vertices; thanks to linearity it reduces to horizontal and vertical increments added during scan-line rasterization.

nodes.label: Perspective Correct Interpolation
nodes.rationale: Interpolation dividing each vertex value by its depth and renormalizing, needed because what is linear in screen space is no longer linear in world space under perspective; both numerator and denominator are barycentric and incremental, and the depth used is the fourth homogeneous component returned by the vertex shader in clipping coordinates.

nodes.label: Face Normal Computation
nodes.rationale: All points of a triangle share one geometric normal, obtainable as the normalized cross product of any two non-aligned vectors on the triangle, e.g. (P3-P1) x (P2-P1).

nodes.label: Vertex Normal Vector
nodes.rationale: Extending a vertex to six values (position plus normal direction) so the normal becomes a property of a (vertex, triangle) couple; it may differ from the geometric triangle normal and even be arbitrary, though fully uncorrelated normals give unnatural shading.

nodes.label: Smooth Shading
nodes.rationale: Combining parameter interpolation with carefully chosen vertex normals so a mesh made of flat faces appears curved; adjacent triangles that share both position and normal direction produce a continuous surface, exactly as storing the original curve normals improves a segmented 2D approximation.

nodes.label: Sharp Edge Encoding
nodes.rationale: Two vertices at the same position but with different normal directions encode a sharp edge; in a cube a single corner belongs to three triangles and therefore needs three distinct 6-tuples.

nodes.label: Normal Renormalization
nodes.rationale: Normals are interpolated component by component, which destroys unit length even when the inputs were unitary, so interpolated normals must be normalized again at every step.

nodes.label: Normal Transformation Matrix
nodes.rationale: Normals are 3D directions, not homogeneous points, so a non-uniform scaling would tilt them the wrong way; the correct 3x3 matrix is the inverse-transpose of the upper-left 3x3 block of the world matrix, and with no scaling or shear the world matrix itself can be used directly.

nodes.label: L11 - UV mapping and Textures
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on how textures parameterize a surface through UV coordinates and how they are addressed and filtered when sampled.

nodes.label: Texture (Map)
nodes.rationale: A table or image assigning shader parameters as a function of the position over a surface, most often the diffuse color but generally any parameter of the BRDF; it avoids giving a distinct material to many small triangles.

nodes.label: Texture Types (1D, 2D, 3D)
nodes.rationale: 2D textures parameterize a surface, 3D textures parameterize a volume, and 1D textures hold precomputed function values or optimizations.

nodes.label: Texel
nodes.rationale: A pixel of a texture, put in correspondence with a point of the object surface by the mapping relation.

nodes.label: UV Mapping
nodes.rationale: The relation associating each triangle of a mesh with a triangle over the planar texture; it need not be a bijection since the same texture region can be reused, unused texture areas are practically unavoidable, and assigning it is a long tedious job for 3D artists.

nodes.label: UV Coordinates
nodes.rationale: Cartesian texture coordinates u and v conventionally varying from 0 to 1 along the horizontal and vertical axes (sometimes named S and T); they are stored only at the vertices as two extra parameters and interpolated for internal points, and the surface and texture triangles need not be similar.

nodes.label: UV-Driven Vertex Duplication
nodes.rationale: As already seen for normal directions, two vertices may share position and even normal but differ in UV, so the seam vertices of a wrapped cylinder must be replicated.

nodes.label: Cube Map
nodes.rationale: Collection of six images indexed by a direction vector whose components pick both the cube side and the texel; the building block for mirror reflection, transparency and realistic indirect lighting.

nodes.label: Clamp Addressing
nodes.rationale: Out-of-range UV handling that extends the border colors to the texels outside [0,1].

nodes.label: Repeat Addressing
nodes.rationale: Out-of-range UV handling that keeps only the fractional part of the coordinates, tiling the pattern.

nodes.label: Mirror Addressing
nodes.rationale: Out-of-range UV handling that tiles the texture but flips it at every repetition.

nodes.label: Constant (Border) Addressing
nodes.rationale: Out-of-range UV handling that replaces samples outside [0,1] with a default color cd; the four strategies can be combined differently on u and v for varied effects.

nodes.label: Texture Filtering
nodes.rationale: Set of techniques reconciling floating-point UV coordinates with integer texel indices and the fact that a screen pixel maps to a complex quad spanning several texels.

nodes.label: Magnification Filtering
nodes.rationale: Case where a texel is larger than the screen pixel, requiring interpolation between nearby texels; only nearest pixel and linear interpolation are defined for it.

nodes.label: Minification Filtering
nodes.rationale: Harder case where one screen pixel covers several texels that should be averaged rather than guessed, motivating mip-mapping, trilinear, rip-mapping and anisotropic filters.

nodes.label: Nearest Pixel Filter
nodes.rationale: Filter that scales u and v by the texture width and height and takes the integer part to index one texel (p[0][0] is top-left in Vulkan); very fast with a single texture read but visibly blocky.

nodes.label: (Bi)linear Interpolation Filter
nodes.rationale: Filter blending the four closest texels, giving smooth results at the price of 4 texture accesses and 3 interpolations; the name bilinear is inaccurate since 1D needs 2 texels and 1 interpolation and 3D needs 8 texels and 7, so it is now simply called linear.

nodes.label: Mip-Mapping
nodes.rationale: Multum In Parvo: a precomputed chain of levels each half the previous, whose texels are averages of the original ones; the algorithm picks the level matching the pixel-to-texel ratio, costs 33% extra memory, and in Vulkan the levels must be created or loaded manually by the developer.

nodes.label: Trilinear Filtering
nodes.rationale: Sampling the two closest mip-map levels and blending them by the texel-to-pixel size difference, removing the visible artifacts caused by an abrupt level change inside an angled triangle.

nodes.label: Rip-Mapping
nodes.rationale: Rectimin Parvo: also stores rectangular rescalings of the texture to fix the under-sampling of one direction that blurs angled surfaces under mip-mapping; it needs 4x memory and is basically never implemented because it still cannot handle angled triangles.

nodes.label: Anisotropic Filtering
nodes.rationale: Unconstrained filter for angled surfaces where a pixel maps to a trapezoid: it picks the mip-map level from the smallest side of the trapezoid and averages up to 8 or 16 samples along the projection direction; very effective but with a large overhead, and optional in Vulkan.

nodes.label: UV Transforming
nodes.rationale: Embedding (u,v) into the homogeneous coordinate (u,v,0,1), multiplying by a texture matrix Mt and dropping the last two components, which allows scaling, rotating or animating a texture and makes the addressing modes essential since the result can leave [0,1].

nodes.label: L12 - Vulkan Rendering Part I
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture introducing the Vulkan rendering process, render passes, pipeline interfaces and vertex data layouts.

nodes.label: The Rendering Process (nested loops)
nodes.rationale: Rendering is organised as nested loops over render passes, pipelines, groups and objects, because changing parameters on the GPU is expensive so objects sharing parameters are grouped together.

nodes.label: Draw Call
nodes.rationale: The instruction that turns a mesh into pixels: vertices go through the Vertex Shader, then every fragment is coloured by the Fragment Shader.

nodes.label: Render Pass
nodes.rationale: A complete rendering of the scene towards a set of targets; different passes may differ in format, purpose and resolution and each needs its own pipeline.

nodes.label: Attachment
nodes.rationale: Each image generated by a render pass is an attachment; one pass can write several attachments of the same size but different format at once.

nodes.label: Depth Buffer Attachment
nodes.rationale: Because Vulkan is explicit, Z-buffering requires a depth attachment beside the colour attachment; these two are the minimum every Vulkan application needs.

nodes.label: Render Subpass
nodes.rationale: Several sub-passes can run on the same attachments and read only the pixel at the identical position, which lets hardware and drivers optimise techniques such as deferred rendering.

nodes.label: Deferred Rendering
nodes.rationale: A technique that first writes geometry data into several attachments and then shades, and which can be optimised with sub-passes.

nodes.label: G-Buffer
nodes.rationale: The set of attachments POSITION, NORMALS, ALBEDO and SPECULAR produced in a single pass.

nodes.label: Shadow Map Pass
nodes.rationale: A first render pass from the light point of view storing distances, used as a texture in the second pass to test whether a point is lit.

nodes.label: Starter.hpp wrapper library
nodes.rationale: Course wrapper library that hides the verbose Vulkan configuration behind classes such as RenderPass, Pipeline, VertexDescriptor, Model, Texture and DescriptorSet.

nodes.label: Pipeline object (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp object that creates a graphics pipeline and loads the shaders named in its initialisation parameters.

nodes.label: RenderPass object (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp object defining a simple render pass that writes to the screen buffer using the z-buffer.

nodes.label: vkCmdDraw()
nodes.rationale: Command that draws non-indexed primitives, used in the first example to draw a triangle on screen.

nodes.label: vkCmdDrawIndexed()
nodes.rationale: Command used to draw a model that also owns an index buffer.

nodes.label: gl_VertexIndex
nodes.rationale: GLSL built-in holding the index of the current vertex, used to hard-code geometry inside the shader.

nodes.label: gl_Position
nodes.rationale: GLSL built-in through which the Vertex Shader returns the normalized screen coordinates of a vertex.

nodes.label: Layout (Vulkan term)
nodes.rationale: Any data structure describing the format and type of user-defined information; the term is heavily overloaded in Vulkan documentation, which causes confusion, and layouts are designed to be reused and mixed between shaders.

nodes.label: Location (shader slot)
nodes.rationale: Numbered slot used to exchange in/out variables between input assembler, vertex shader, fragment shader and framebuffer; only the number matters, not the variable name.

nodes.label: Pipeline Interfaces
nodes.rationale: Configuring what data flows between application, vertex shader, fragment shader and attachments is the main development effort in Vulkan.

nodes.label: Vertex Data
nodes.rationale: Data attached to vertices: positions, normals, UV coordinates, colours, tangents, bones and weights.

nodes.label: Intra-Shader Data
nodes.rationale: Values the vertex shader passes to the fragment shader, such as interpolated normals, world positions and UVs.

nodes.label: CPU to Shader Data
nodes.rationale: Parameters the application sends to shaders: transform matrices, light definitions, viewer position, material properties and textures.

nodes.label: Input Assembler
nodes.rationale: Fixed pipeline stage that feeds vertex attribute values into the in variables of the vertex shader, configured at pipeline creation.

nodes.label: Vertex Shader
nodes.rationale: Programmable stage that transforms each vertex and is the only stage able to access vertex attributes directly.

nodes.label: Fragment Shader
nodes.rationale: Programmable stage computing the final colour of every fragment; its out variables correspond to the attachments of the render pass.

nodes.label: Perspective Correct Interpolation
nodes.rationale: Default interpolation applied by the fixed functions to the out variables of the vertex shader before the fragment shader reads them.

nodes.label: flat and noperspective qualifiers
nodes.rationale: GLSL directives placed before in/out variables to switch off or change the default perspective correct interpolation.

nodes.label: Vertex Attributes
nodes.rationale: Arbitrary user-defined per-vertex values; all vertices of a mesh drawn by one pipeline must share the same format, so different formats need different pipelines.

nodes.label: Vertex Binding
nodes.rationale: Each array into which vertex data can be split is a binding with its own progressive id, independent from the location ids; Starter.hpp currently supports a single binding.

nodes.label: Vertex Input Descriptor
nodes.rationale: VkVertexInputAttributeDescription entries giving binding, location, format and offset for each field of the C++ Vertex structure; filling them by hand is verbose copy-paste work.

nodes.label: VertexDescriptor (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp structure whose init() takes the bindings (id, stride, input rate) and the locations (binding, location, format, offset, size, usage) that define the vertex layout.

nodes.label: VkFormat constants
nodes.rationale: Format enumerations such as VK_FORMAT_R32G32B32_SFLOAT used for attributes; not all formats are supported on every platform.

nodes.label: VertexDescriptorElementUsage
nodes.rationale: Enumeration (POSITION, NORMAL, UV, COLOR, TANGENT, POS2D, JOINTWEIGHT, JOINTINDEX, OTHER) that is ignored by Vulkan but tells the Starter.hpp model loader where to put each property read from a file.

nodes.label: Model (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp data structure holding a mesh, whose vertices and indices can be filled in code or loaded from a file through init() with a VertexDescriptor pointer.

nodes.label: Model file formats (OBJ, GLTF, MGCG)
nodes.rationale: OBJ supports position, normal, one UV channel and vertex colour; GLTF adds multiple UV channels and tangents; MGCG is a course-specific GLTF wrapper created to distribute third party assets without violating copyright licences.

nodes.label: Index Buffer
nodes.rationale: Buffer of vertex indices with a fixed format, required to draw indexed primitives.

nodes.label: Triangle Lists and Strips
nodes.rationale: The two encodings used to send primitives to the pipeline; strips reuse vertices and therefore need much less memory than lists.

nodes.label: L13 - Vulkan Rendering Part II
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on how the application communicates with shaders through uniform buffers, descriptor set layouts, descriptor sets, pipeline layouts and descriptor pools.

nodes.label: Uniform Buffer
nodes.rationale: Block of scene- and mesh-dependent data sent from the application to the shaders through uniform global variables.

nodes.label: Push Constants
nodes.rationale: Alternative, announced-for-later mechanism to send parameters from the application to a shader, with its own features and limitations.

nodes.label: Uniform Block (UniformBufferObject)
nodes.rationale: A C++ struct in RAM mirroring, in the same order and types, the uniform block declared in the shader.

nodes.label: Uniform Alignment Requirements (alignas)
nodes.rationale: GPU memory has stricter alignment than RAM so the C++ struct must use alignas (4 for float, 8 for vec2, 16 for vec3/vec4/mat3/mat4); mat3 should be avoided because some Vulkan implementations mishandle 3x3 matrices.

nodes.label: Descriptor Set ID (Set)
nodes.rationale: Vulkan groups uniforms into sets whose id expresses the update frequency, with lower ids assumed to change less often.

nodes.label: Binding (uniform resource index)
nodes.rationale: Secondary index identifying each resource inside a set, starting from zero.

nodes.label: Uniform Update Frequency Hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Parameters are split by how often they change (scene, pipeline, material, object) so that GPU state changes are minimised and meshes with identical settings are drawn one after the other.

nodes.label: Descriptor Types
nodes.rationale: Kinds of resource accessible as uniforms: uniform block, texture sampler, image, combined image and sampler, render pass attachment.

nodes.label: Descriptor Set Layout
nodes.rationale: The class of a group of uniforms: it declares descriptor types, binding ids and the shader stages where they are used.

nodes.label: Descriptor Set
nodes.rationale: The instance of a descriptor set layout holding actual values, so meshes needing different world matrices use different descriptor sets of the same layout.

nodes.label: Pipeline Layout
nodes.rationale: Selects which descriptor set layouts a pipeline's shaders can access and at which set id, so different pipelines can see the same descriptor sets at different ids.

nodes.label: Descriptor Pool
nodes.rationale: Pre-sized allocator from which descriptor sets are taken; sizing it correctly is hard and depends on the engine, so the course tolerates overprovisioning even though production code must avoid it.

nodes.label: DPSZs (Descriptor Pool SiZes)
nodes.rationale: Global Starter.hpp object whose fields give the sizes used when creating the descriptor pool.

nodes.label: DescriptorSetLayout class (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp class configured with init() taking one definition per binding, each with index, descriptor type, shader stages, linkSize and count.

nodes.label: DescriptorSet class (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp class whose init() receives the DescriptorSetLayout pointer and an array of textures, which may be empty when no texture is used.

nodes.label: Shader Stage Flags
nodes.rationale: VK_SHADER_STAGE_VERTEX_BIT, VK_SHADER_STAGE_FRAGMENT_BIT and VK_SHADER_STAGE_ALL_GRAPHICS select where a descriptor is visible.

nodes.label: linkSize and count fields
nodes.rationale: linkSize means the byte size for a uniform buffer binding or the texture array position for a texture binding, while count creates arrays of descriptors.

nodes.label: map() method
nodes.rationale: Descriptor Set method that copies the filled C++ uniform structure to the shader, given the pointer to the object and the binding number.

nodes.label: Material (BRDF parameter set)
nodes.rationale: The parameters that configure a BRDF (specular power, roughness, diffuse and specular colours, textures) grouped as one uniform update frequency.

nodes.label: L14 - Vulkan Rendering Part III
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo
nodes.rationale: Lecture on textures and samplers in Vulkan: preparation and transition, Starter.hpp Texture and TextureSampler classes, cube maps and texture arrays.

nodes.label: Texture
nodes.rationale: The table holding the texel values, which can use many different encodings.

nodes.label: Sampler
nodes.rationale: Object describing how texels are read: filtering algorithms and the policy for UV values outside the 0..1 range.

nodes.label: Combined Texture and Sampler
nodes.rationale: Since texture and sampler must both always exist they are usually merged into one uniform of type sampler1D/2D/3D/Cube inside the shader.

nodes.label: Texture Unit
nodes.rationale: Dedicated GPU hardware block performing the interpolations and floating point work of texture sampling, which requires data in its own internal format.

nodes.label: Staging Buffer
nodes.rationale: Intermediate GPU-accessible memory area through which a loaded image passes before being moved into its final texture memory.

nodes.label: Image Layout Transition
nodes.rationale: Converting texel organisation and colour format from one Layout to another, a step Vulkan requires to be explicit and that Starter.hpp implements internally; the verb to Transition is confusing terminology for non-native speakers.

nodes.label: stb_image / stbi_load()
nodes.rationale: External library used by Starter.hpp to load an image file into an RGBA pixel array together with its size, from which mip levels are computed.

nodes.label: Texture class (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp class whose init() loads a texture from file; textures can also come from a previous render pass or be generated in code.

nodes.label: TextureSampler class (Starter.hpp)
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp object defining a custom sampler (filters, address modes, mipmap mode, anisotropy) which is attached to a texture with setSampler().

nodes.label: Magnification and Minification Filters
nodes.rationale: magFilter and minFilter select VK_FILTER_NEAREST or VK_FILTER_LINEAR interpolation of texels.

nodes.label: Sampler Address Modes
nodes.rationale: addressModeU and addressModeV choose repeat, mirrored repeat or clamp to edge behaviour for UV outside 0..1.

nodes.label: Mip-mapping (mipmapMode, maxLod)
nodes.rationale: Reduced-resolution image levels selected with nearest or linear mipmap mode, disabled by setting maxLod to zero.

nodes.label: Anisotropic Filtering
nodes.rationale: Enabled with anisotropyEnable and bounded by maxAnisotropy; it is the default minification filter of the standard sampler.

nodes.label: texture() GLSL function
nodes.rationale: Reads a colour from a sampler at given coordinates and returns a vec4 whose last component is the alpha channel.

nodes.label: textureLod()
nodes.rationale: Samples a mip-mapped image at an explicitly chosen minification level, with 0 being the highest detail.

nodes.label: Non-color Texture Format (SRGB vs UNORM)
nodes.rationale: The default VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_SRGB applies gamma correction, which biases non-colour data such as normal maps, so those textures must be created with VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM.

nodes.label: Cube Map (initCubic, samplerCube)
nodes.rationale: Texture built from six side images with initCubic() and sampled in the shader through a samplerCube using a direction vector.

nodes.label: Arrays of Textures
nodes.rationale: Declared with count greater than one in the descriptor set layout and occupying N consecutive positions in the texture array; the shader index must itself be a uniform unless extensions are used.

nodes.label: Separate Texture and Sampler
nodes.rationale: Using VK_DESCRIPTOR_TYPE_SAMPLER and VK_DESCRIPTOR_TYPE_SAMPLED_IMAGE at different array indices, the shader recombines a texture* image and a sampler to read texels, and the pool must size samplersInPool and sampledImagesInPool.

nodes.label: Texture Binding Lifetime in Descriptor Sets
nodes.rationale: Unlike uniforms that can be re-mapped every frame, a texture stays fixed for the whole life of the descriptor set and therefore must be passed as an array of pointers at descriptor set creation.
nodes.norm_label: texture binding lifetime in descriptor sets

nodes.label: L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lecture completing pipeline creation (viewport, scissor, rasterizer, depth-stencil, multisampling, blending), render pass objects and command buffer recording.
nodes.norm_label: l15 - pipelines, render passes and command buffers

nodes.label: Vulkan Graphics Pipeline
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: The most complex and important data structure of the whole 3D visualization process, gathering input assembler, vertex input, shader stages and all fixed-function state.

nodes.label: Viewport (VkViewport)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Rectangular area in pixels where the normalized screen coordinates (-1,-1)..(1,1) are mapped, with minDepth and maxDepth for the z range.

nodes.label: Scissor Test (VkRect2D)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Rectangle that cuts away part of the surface so that an area of the screen stays unaffected by Vulkan, for example to host a GUI.

nodes.label: Rasterization State (VkPipelineRasterizationStateCreateInfo)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Configures the rasterizer: polygon mode (fill or wireframe), line width, culling and depth bias.

nodes.label: Back-face Culling (cullMode, frontFace)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Switched with VK_CULL_MODE_BACK_BIT or VK_CULL_MODE_NONE, while frontFace states whether clockwise or counter-clockwise vertex order faces the viewer.

nodes.label: Depth and Stencil State (VkPipelineDepthStencilStateCreateInfo)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Enables depth test and depth write and chooses the comparison operator (for example VK_COMPARE_OP_LESS) plus the optional stencil test.

nodes.label: Multisampling (VkPipelineMultisampleStateCreateInfo)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Anti-aliasing configuration that must be filled even when no anti-aliasing is used.

nodes.label: Color Blending
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Per colour attachment state deciding whether a new fragment colour replaces or is combined with the one already stored, collected in VkPipelineColorBlendStateCreateInfo.

nodes.label: VkRenderPass
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Object collecting in a single structure everything needed to perform a rendering producing the same output data on the considered geometry.

nodes.label: VkAttachmentDescription
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Describes one attachment: its format, sample count, load and store operations, stencil operations and initial and final image layouts.

nodes.label: Depth Attachment description
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Attachment whose format comes from findDepthFormat(physicalDevice) and which ends in VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_OPTIMAL to support Z-buffering.

nodes.label: VkAttachmentReference
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Wraps the id of an attachment and the image layout in which it will be used.

nodes.label: VkSubpassDescription
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Describes one complete rendering cycle, its pipeline bind point and the colour and depth-stencil attachment references it uses.

nodes.label: VkSubpassDependency
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Synchronization primitive between sub-passes expressed with source and destination subpass, stage masks and access masks.

nodes.label: vkCreateRenderPass() / VkRenderPassCreateInfo
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Collects attachments, sub-passes and dependencies and creates the VkRenderPass object on the logical device.

nodes.label: RenderPass configuration in Starter.hpp
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: By default creates a single pass with depth buffer and antialiasing connected to the presentation swap chain, with standard attachment and dependency sets retrievable by keyword through getStandarAttachmentsProperties() and getStandardDependencies().

nodes.label: getViewAndSampler()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Starter.hpp function passing the image view and sampler of an extra colour attachment to a descriptor set in the slot reserved for a texture.

nodes.label: Swap Chain
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: The presentation chain of images whose framebuffers and extent are used by the default render pass and by vkCmdBeginRenderPass.

nodes.label: Framebuffer
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: The memory area where the out values produced by the Fragment Shader are finally stored, specified when beginning a render pass.

nodes.label: Command Buffer
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Vulkan stores all graphics commands into command buffers that are later submitted to a queue for execution.

nodes.label: Queue submission
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Recorded command buffers are handed to a queue, which is what actually executes them on the device.

nodes.label: vkBeginCommandBuffer() / vkEndCommandBuffer()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Open and close the recording of commands into a command buffer.

nodes.label: vkCmdBeginRenderPass() / vkCmdEndRenderPass()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Delimit the commands that draw; the begin info names the render pass, the framebuffer, the render area and the clear values for colour and depth.

nodes.label: Resource Binding in the Command Buffer
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Before drawing, the pipeline, vertex buffer, index buffer and descriptor sets must be bound; bindings stay valid until replaced, so drawing many objects with one pipeline only requires rebinding buffers and descriptor sets.
nodes.norm_label: resource binding in the command buffer

nodes.label: vkCmdBindPipeline()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Binds a graphics pipeline to the command buffer at the graphics bind point.

nodes.label: Vertex Buffer / vkCmdBindVertexBuffers()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: GPU buffer holding vertex data, bound with an offset so that several primitives can share the same buffer for better performance.
