nodes.label: vkCmdBindIndexBuffer()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Binds the index buffer with an offset and an index type of 16 or 32 bits.

nodes.label: vkCmdBindDescriptorSets()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Binds an array of consecutive descriptor sets, given the pipeline bind point, the pipeline layout and the first set index.

nodes.label: vkCmdDraw() (non-indexed)
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Used for plain triangle lists or strips, where binding an index buffer is not necessary.

nodes.label: vkCmdDrawIndexed()
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Draws indexed primitives taking the index count, instance count, first index, vertex offset and first instance, which allows packing several meshes in one index buffer.

nodes.label: Instancing
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Repeated objects sharing geometry and shaders are stored once and drawn many times, each copy using its own world matrix.

nodes.label: gl_InstanceIndex
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Built-in variable giving the id of the copy being drawn, used to fetch the parameters of that instance.

nodes.label: Pipeline defaults in Starter.hpp
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: Pipelines are created with entire-screen viewport, no scissor, back-face culling on, filled triangles, no transparency and indexed triangle lists, and are initialised with the descriptor set layouts and the .SPV shader binaries.

nodes.label: Command buffer population in Starter.hpp
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: A static function fills the command buffer and is passed to a submit procedure; each buffer has a name (resubmitting the same name replaces it) and an order id that sorts execution, so an overlay can be drawn above the scene.

nodes.label: Physical Device
nodes.source_file: Lessons/L15 - Pipelines, Render Passes and Command Buffers.txt
nodes.rationale: The GPU queried, for instance by findDepthFormat(physicalDevice), to know which formats it supports.

nodes.label: E01 - GLM and Projections Types
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lab deck introducing the GLM linear-algebra library and the full family of parallel, axonometric, oblique and perspective projection matrices, with the corrections needed to use OpenGL-oriented GLM functions in Vulkan.

nodes.label: GLM library
nodes.rationale: A header-only C++ linear algebra library that uses GLSL type names and C++ operator overloading, created for OpenGL but usable with Vulkan, so matrix maths in the application mirrors the shader code.

nodes.label: GLM header inclusion (glm.hpp, matrix_transform.hpp)
nodes.rationale: glm/glm.hpp must be included first and glm/gtc/matrix_transform.hpp adds the transform-matrix constructors.

nodes.label: glm::mat4
nodes.rationale: The 4x4 matrix type used to encode transforms: built column-by-column, indexed as [column][row], multiplied with *, and glm::mat4(1) yields the identity.

nodes.label: glm::inverse and glm::transpose
nodes.rationale: GLM inverts a matrix with inverse(...) and transposes it with transpose(...).

nodes.label: glm::vec3 and glm::vec4
nodes.rationale: Three- and four-component vector types that combine with matrices through the conventional + - * operators.

nodes.label: glm::translate
nodes.rationale: Builds a 4x4 translation matrix of displacement (dx, dy, dz) starting from an existing matrix, usually glm::mat4(1).

nodes.label: glm::scale
nodes.rationale: Builds a 4x4 scaling matrix with factors (sx, sy, sz), with a one-argument shortcut for proportional scaling.

nodes.label: glm::rotate
nodes.rationale: Builds a rotation matrix of a given angle around an arbitrary axis vector; passing (1,0,0), (0,1,0) or (0,0,1) gives the x, y and z axis rotations.

nodes.label: GLM_FORCE_RADIANS and glm::radians()
nodes.rationale: Angles should be expressed in radians by defining GLM_FORCE_RADIANS before including GLM and converting degrees with glm::radians(); C++ literals must carry a .0f or f suffix to be floating point.

nodes.label: GLM shear functions (shearX3D, shearY3D, shearZ3D)
nodes.rationale: Shear transforms require the extra header glm/gtx/transform2.hpp and are the building block of oblique projections.

nodes.label: Orthogonal projection matrix
nodes.rationale: Composed in three steps as Mort * Sort * Tort: translate the near-plane centre of the projection box to the origin, scale coordinates into the normalized range, then mirror the y and z axes to match the screen conventions.

nodes.label: glm::ortho
nodes.rationale: Computes the orthographic projection matrix from the l, r, b, t, n, f boundaries of the visible region in world coordinates.

nodes.label: Vulkan corrections for GLM projections
nodes.rationale: GLM projection functions follow OpenGL conventions, so Vulkan needs GLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE to put z in [0,1] plus a y-axis flip, obtained either by pre-multiplying a scale(1,-1,1) or, for perspective, by negating element [1][1].

nodes.label: Axonometric projections
nodes.rationale: Parallel projections that keep the up axis (y) parallel to the vertical direction of the screen, popular in games like Monument Valley, SimCity 4 and Fallout.

nodes.label: Isometric projection
nodes.rationale: The three axes are 120 degrees apart and equal 3D lengths stay equal on screen; obtained by rotating +/-45 degrees about y then +/-35.26 degrees about x before the parallel projection, whose matrix is then given via half-width and aspect ratio.

nodes.label: Dimetric projection
nodes.rationale: Two different units, one for x and z and one for y, obtained by a +/-45 degree y rotation followed by an arbitrary x rotation; it was widespread in 80s arcade and home games because it needs only integer arithmetic.

nodes.label: Trimetric projection
nodes.rationale: Allows a different unit on each of the three axes, obtained with arbitrary rotations about y and then x before the parallel projection.

nodes.label: Oblique projections
nodes.rationale: Keep the x and y axes parallel to the screen and angle z (typically 30, 45 or 60 degrees); implemented as a shear along z applied before the orthogonal projection, where the shear factor sets both the angle and the depth reduction.

nodes.label: Cavalier and Cabinet projections
nodes.rationale: Two oblique variants: Cavalier keeps the z-axis unit length (reduction factor 1), Cabinet halves it (factor 0.5), both usually at a 45 degree angle.

nodes.label: Perspective projection matrix
nodes.rationale: Built as Mpersp * Spersp * Tpersp * Upersp from the near/far distances and the l, r, t, b edges of the projection plane at the near plane, producing the classic matrix with -1 in the off-diagonal position.

nodes.label: glm::frustum
nodes.rationale: Computes the perspective projection matrix from the six boundary values l, r, b, t, n, f.

nodes.label: glm::perspective
nodes.rationale: Computes the perspective projection matrix from vertical field of view, aspect ratio and the near and far plane distances - the usual camera-oriented parameterisation.

nodes.label: FOV / aspect ratio to frustum boundaries
nodes.rationale: The frustum edges follow from the field of view and aspect ratio as t = n*tan(fov/2), b = -t, r = a*t, l = -r, so that r-l = a*(t-b).
nodes.norm_label: fov / aspect ratio to frustum boundaries

nodes.label: E02 - Matrices Wrap up
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lab deck wrapping up view, world and projection matrices in GLM, including quaternion rotations and a fully worked numerical World-View-Projection example.

nodes.label: Look-in-direction view matrix in GLM
nodes.rationale: GLM has no dedicated helper, so the view matrix is built by hand as the inverse of the camera matrix, Rz(-rho)*Rx(-beta)*Ry(-alpha)*T(-c), i.e. inverse rotations in reverse order applied after a negative translation.

nodes.label: Look-at view matrix
nodes.rationale: Built from camera position c, target a and up vector u by normalizing vz = c-a, vx = normalize(cross(u,vz)) and vy = cross(vz,vx), assembling the camera matrix by columns and inverting it.

nodes.label: glm::lookAt
nodes.rationale: Ready-made GLM function producing the look-at view matrix from the camera centre, the target point and the up vector.

nodes.label: glm::cross, glm::normalize and column constructor
nodes.rationale: cross() gives the vector product, normalize() makes a vector unitary, and glm::mat4 can be built directly from four column vectors - the three primitives needed to assemble a camera frame.

nodes.label: Roll in look-at matrices
nodes.rationale: Roll can be added either by rotating the up vector u itself or by pre-multiplying the look-at matrix with a rotation of -Roll around the z-axis.

nodes.label: World matrix in GLM
nodes.rationale: GLM offers no single world-matrix helper, so it is more practical to write the whole sequence translate * yaw * pitch * roll * scale explicitly rather than rely on eulerAngleYXZ.

nodes.label: Euler angles and glm::eulerAngleYXZ
nodes.rationale: The glm/gtx/euler_angles.hpp package builds a rotation matrix from yaw, pitch and roll in the YXZ order used by the course convention.

nodes.label: Quaternion rotations
nodes.rationale: Relative orientation changes are encoded as unitary quaternions combining rotation axis and amount, e.g. a 6 degree turn about y becomes cos(3)+sin(3)*j, and are applied by quaternion multiplication.

nodes.label: World-space vs local-space quaternion rotation
nodes.rationale: Putting the rotation quaternion first rotates around the current world axes, putting it last rotates around the object's own modelling axes - the choice decides whether controls feel global or local.

nodes.label: glm::quat
nodes.rationale: Quaternions come from glm/gtc/quaternion.hpp and can be built from Euler angles (pitch, yaw, roll order), from scalar plus i/j/k components, or from axis and angle via rotate(); .w is the scalar part, .x/.y/.z the vector part, glm::mat4(q) converts to a rotation matrix and normalize() restores unit length.

nodes.label: Quaternion Euler-order caveat
nodes.rationale: The glm::quat Euler constructor uses the rarely wanted pitch-yaw-roll order, so for the course's zxy convention the three base quaternions must be composed manually.

nodes.label: World matrix from a quaternion
nodes.rationale: With a quaternion orientation the world matrix collapses to translate(pos) * mat4(q) * scale(s), simpler than chaining three Euler rotations.

nodes.label: World-View-Projection matrix
nodes.rationale: The World, View and Projection matrices are usually factorised into a single MWVP = MP * MV * MW so that local coordinates reach clipping space with one product.

nodes.label: Five transform steps (World, View, Projection, Normalization, Screen)
nodes.rationale: Model coordinates become pixels through a fixed chain of spaces - local, world, camera, clipping, normalized screen, screen - where the first three (and possibly the last) are matrix products while normalization is a division that cannot be folded into them.
nodes.norm_label: five transform steps (world, view, projection, normalization, screen)

nodes.label: Perspective division (normalization step)
nodes.rationale: Clipping coordinates become normalized screen coordinates by dividing every component by w and dropping the fourth; parallel projections skip this since MP-Ort already yields normalized coordinates.

nodes.label: Screen transform to pixel coordinates
nodes.rationale: Normalized coordinates map to pixels with xS = (Sw-1)/2 * (1+xn) and yS = (Sh-1)/2 * (1-yn); the driver performs this step transparently.

nodes.label: Clipping coordinates
nodes.rationale: The homogeneous space produced by a perspective projection before the division by w; it is what a 3D application hands to the underlying framework.

nodes.label: Complete projection example (tetrahedron starship)
nodes.rationale: A worked numerical walkthrough that projects a wireframe tetrahedron ship onto a simulated 960x540 screen with 5:4 aspect and 90 degree FOV, computing the world matrix from Euler angles, the view matrix by look-in-direction, the projection matrix, then clipping, normalized and pixel coordinates.

nodes.label: E03 - Mesh construction
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lab deck on how meshes are stored and drawn: indexed primitives and their memory cost, back-face culling, screen synchronization with double and triple buffering, and the clipping algorithm.

nodes.label: Indexed primitives
nodes.rationale: Storing each vertex once and referring to it through an index array shrinks a cube from 432 to 168 bytes without the ordering headaches of strips, which is why most interchange formats only support indexed triangle lists.

nodes.label: Triangle strip
nodes.rationale: Encoding a cube as a strip needs only 14 vertices (six of them repeated) instead of 36, but requires finding a valid ordering.

nodes.label: Primitive restart
nodes.rationale: Vulkan lets a negative index restart the strip, so band-like structures can be packed into a single index array (a cube in 20 indices, 136 bytes total).

nodes.label: Wireframe indexed primitives and outlines
nodes.rationale: Line lists can be indexed too (a cube's 12 lines drop from 288 to 120 bytes), and Vulkan can also draw ordinary meshes as triangle contours.

nodes.label: Back-face culling
nodes.rationale: Faces pointing away from the viewer are discarded by checking whether the projected vertices run clockwise or counterclockwise; Vulkan does this in normalized screen coordinates using only the sign of the z component of (v3-v2) x (v2-v1).

nodes.label: Winding order conventions and culling pitfalls
nodes.rationale: The culling test must be user-selectable and inverted when the world matrix scales with an odd number of negative factors; culling also breaks for non 2-manifold or transparent objects, and enclosing geometry such as a room or skybox must be built with reversed winding so its inner faces stay visible.
nodes.norm_label: winding order conventions and culling pitfalls

nodes.label: Screen synchronization and Vsync
nodes.rationale: CPU, GPU and display run at independent speeds, so an application should start updating only after the Vsync interrupt the adapter raises at the end of each screen trace.

nodes.label: Tearing
nodes.rationale: A visible break in the animation caused by the adapter reading video memory while the program is still composing the image.

nodes.label: Double buffering
nodes.rationale: Two frame buffers let the application draw into the back buffer while the adapter shows the front one, swapping at Vsync - effective, but it caps the frame rate at the monitor refresh and idles CPU and GPU.

nodes.label: Triple buffering
nodes.rationale: A third buffer decouples the application from the presentation so it never waits for Vsync, allowing frame rates above the display rate at the cost of extra memory and of wasting work on frames that get skipped.

nodes.label: Frame skipping
nodes.rationale: If a new frame is finished before the next Vsync the previous one is never displayed, which keeps animation smooth and tearing-free while discarding surplus frames.

nodes.label: Clipping
nodes.rationale: Truncating or discarding primitives so they fit inside the screen; performed against the viewing frustum after the projection transform but before the division by w, hence the name clipping coordinates.

nodes.label: Half-spaces and frustum planes
nodes.rationale: A plane written in homogeneous form n = (nx,ny,nz,d) turns the plane equation into a scalar product n.p whose sign selects a half-space and whose value is the signed distance; the convex frustum is the intersection of six such half-spaces with fixed normals in clipping space.

nodes.label: Point clipping test
nodes.rationale: A point is inside the frustum only if its scalar product with all six plane normals is positive, so one negative product is enough to discard it.

nodes.label: Triangle clipping algorithm
nodes.rationale: Per plane the three signed distances give a trivial accept or reject; otherwise intersections are interpolated using the distances as coefficients, producing one replacement triangle when two vertices are outside and two triangles when only one is, and each result is then clipped against the next plane.

nodes.label: Cost of clipping
nodes.rationale: Triangles can double at every plane, so the storage must hold a variable number of figures and each intersection must interpolate every vertex attribute (normals, colours, UVs), which is why drivers hide this step from the user.

nodes.label: E04 - Controls and Navigation
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lab deck on camera navigation: the Walk and Fly models, six-axis input normalization, GLFW input handling, third-person camera placement for ships and characters, and damping of camera and character motion.

nodes.label: Camera navigation models
nodes.rationale: Motion in 3D has six axes (three translation, three rotation) and two main models exploit them: Walk, for environments with a ground and gravity, and Fly, for free open space such as a starship in orbit.

nodes.label: Six-axis control values (mx, my, mz, rx, ry, rz)
nodes.rationale: A navigation update receives up to six floats: mx, my, mz for movement along the horizontal, vertical and depth axes and rx, ry, rz for rotation around them.
nodes.norm_label: six-axis control values (mx, my, mz, rx, ry, rz)

nodes.label: Control axis normalization to [-1, +1]
nodes.rationale: Every input device is wrapped to return -1, 0 or +1 per axis so the navigation code is device independent: discrete sources (keys, buttons, hat switches, DPads) map to the three values, continuous ones (thumbsticks, triggers, mouse) return any float in the range depending on intensity.

nodes.label: Walk navigation model
nodes.rationale: Keeps the camera state as a position vector plus the three angles alpha, beta, rho and rebuilds a Look-In-Direction view matrix every frame; only the yaw affects the direction of motion, while pitch and roll act on the view alone.

nodes.label: Unitary movement vectors ux, uy, uz
nodes.rationale: ux = Ry(alpha)*(1,0,0,1).xyz and uz = Ry(alpha)*(0,0,1,1).xyz turn with the yaw while uy stays (0,1,0), so strafing and forward motion follow the gaze but vertical motion stays world-aligned.
nodes.norm_label: unitary movement vectors ux, uy, uz

nodes.label: Linear and angular speed with delta time
nodes.rationale: Motion is scaled by a linear speed mu in world units per second and an angular speed omega in radians per second, both multiplied by the elapsed time dt so the animation is frame-rate independent.
nodes.norm_label: linear and angular speed with delta time

nodes.label: Walk model update cycle
nodes.rationale: Each frame the angles accumulate omega*r*dt, the position accumulates ux/uy/uz * mu * m * dt, and a fresh view matrix is rebuilt with MakeLookAt(pos, alpha, beta, rho) - keeping explicit state is easier than editing the matrix in place.

nodes.label: Fly navigation model
nodes.rationale: Stores only the view matrix and updates it directly, applying translations and rotations along the camera-space axes in the opposite direction to the intended movement because the view matrix is the inverse of the camera matrix.

nodes.label: Order of incremental transforms
nodes.rationale: Matrix products do not commute, but in the Fly update the order rarely shows because usually only one of the six axis values is non-zero and the per-frame increments are nearly infinitesimal.

nodes.label: Recovering the viewer position
nodes.rationale: The rendering equation needs the camera position: in the Walk model it is already stored, in the Fly model it is extracted as glm::vec3(glm::inverse(ViewMatrix) * glm::vec4(0,0,0,1)).

nodes.label: GLFW
nodes.rationale: An open source multi-platform C library for OpenGL and Vulkan that creates windows and delivers input and events, chosen over SDL for this course; window creation returns a GLFWwindow* used by every later call.

nodes.label: GLFW input functions (glfwGetKey, glfwGetCursorPos, glfwGetMouseButton)
nodes.rationale: glfwGetKey reports whether a named key was pressed since the last call, glfwGetCursorPos writes the mouse position in pixels into two doubles, and glfwGetMouseButton returns GLFW_PRESS for a named button.

nodes.label: Converting mouse motion to axis values
nodes.rationale: Take the difference with the previous cursor position, held in static variables, and divide by a movement-resolution constant (ideally window-size dependent) to land in the [-1,+1] range.
nodes.norm_label: converting mouse motion to axis values

nodes.label: Frame delta time with <chrono>
nodes.rationale: Platform-independent motion needs the time since the previous call, obtained with the C++ <chrono> high-resolution clock by storing the previous timestamp in a static variable and taking the difference in seconds.

nodes.label: getSixAxis() in Starter.hpp
nodes.rationale: The course framework wraps all input into one call filling a float with the seconds since the previous frame, a vec3 of motion axes, a vec3 of rotation axes and a boolean fire flag, with keyboard and mouse mapped onto those axes.

nodes.label: Third-person camera placement
nodes.rationale: The user drives a main actor and the camera follows, so three positions must be derived each frame - the object, the camera and the camera target, the latter usually tied to the object.

nodes.label: Third-person spaceship camera
nodes.rationale: The ship's world matrix is updated in local coordinates like a Fly camera; the target is the ship itself, the camera centre is MW*(0,0,d,1).xyz at a fixed distance d and the up vector is MW*(0,1,0,0).xyz, i.e. the ship's own y-axis.

nodes.label: Local/global coordinates model in quaternion form
nodes.rationale: Orientation kept as a quaternion is more compact: rot is post-multiplied by per-axis rotation quaternions, the three axis directions are read back from mat4(rot), position accumulates along them, and the world matrix is rebuilt with MakeWorldQuat(pos, rot).
nodes.norm_label: local/global coordinates model in quaternion form

nodes.label: Ground motion model
nodes.rationale: The third-person equivalent of the Walk cycle applied to the controlled object: position plus yaw, pitch and roll are stored, ux and uz follow the yaw (with uz built from (0,0,-1,1)), and the world matrix comes from MakeWorldEuler; in most cases only yaw is actually needed.

nodes.label: Third-person character camera
nodes.rationale: For a character the target sits at a height h above the origin at the feet, the camera orbits at distance d with pitch theta as c = MW*(0, h + d*sin(theta), d*cos(theta), 1).xyz while a = MW*(0,0,0,1).xyz + (0,0,h) and the up vector stays (0,1,0).

nodes.label: Camera damping
nodes.rationale: Moving the camera centre instantly looks unnatural, so the new position is blended exponentially over time as p = pOLD*exp(-lambda*dt) + pNEW*(1-exp(-lambda*dt)), with a damping speed lambda around 10 giving good results; the same filter can also smooth the object's own position.

nodes.label: Damped character facing direction
nodes.rationale: In professional player controllers the movement direction is independent of the view: relDir = Yaw + atan2(-m.x, m.z) is computed only when the stick is actually pushed, wrapped to stay within +/-pi of the damped value, then exponentially damped and used to rotate the character's world matrix about y.

nodes.label: E05 - GLSL and Shaders
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione
nodes.rationale: Lab deck introducing SPIR-V and the GLSL language: how shaders are compiled, the language syntax and types, GPU flow-control caveats, and how shaders talk to the pipeline and to the application.

nodes.label: SPIR-V
nodes.rationale: Standard Portable Intermediate Representation, the binary device-independent format Vulkan shaders are defined in; each driver translates it to its GPU's own instructions cheaply because SPIR-V was designed for that.

nodes.label: GLSL
nodes.rationale: The OpenGL Shading Language, a C-like high level language used in this course to write the BRDF, indirect light and emission models later implemented in shaders; the alternative is Microsoft's HLSL.

nodes.label: glslc compiler
nodes.rationale: The Vulkan SDK tool that compiles a GLSL source file into a .spv binary, invoked with the source name followed by -o and the output file; correct installations put it on the command path.

nodes.label: Shader source and binary file extensions
nodes.rationale: Each shader stage has its own conventional GLSL source extension, while every compiled SPIR-V file uses .spv.
nodes.norm_label: shader source and binary file extensions

nodes.label: GLSL program structure
nodes.rationale: A shader holds global definitions and functions at file scope with main() as the usual entry point, must begin with a #version directive asking at least for 450, and uses C comment and brace conventions.

nodes.label: GLSL data types (scalars, vecn, matn)
nodes.rationale: Beyond C scalar types GLSL offers 2/3/4 component vectors, widely used for colours and coordinates, and 2x2/3x3/4x4 single-precision matrices stored column-major and indexed with [ ][ ], whose columns can be read as vectors.

nodes.label: Vector component aliases and swizzling
nodes.rationale: Components are reached with dot syntax and each has aliases for position, colour and texture use, and the order can be shuffled, as in light.zxy = light.xyz.

nodes.label: GLM / GLSL type correspondence
nodes.rationale: GLM deliberately mirrors GLSL type names in C++ so data can move between application code and shaders without mental translation.

nodes.label: Vector/matrix literals and type casting
nodes.rationale: Values are constructed by writing the type name with a comma-separated list, larger vectors can be assembled from shorter ones, and the same syntax performs explicit casts.

nodes.label: GLSL functions, conditionals and loops
nodes.rationale: GLSL keeps the C operator set, function declaration and call syntax, if/else and the ?: form, for and while loops, and the usual loop exit statements.

nodes.label: SIMD flow-control caveat on GPUs
nodes.rationale: Because the GPU is SIMD, both branches of an if are always executed and a variable-length loop costs as much as the longest iteration in the batch, so branches and variable loops should be avoided.

nodes.label: Shader-pipeline communication: in and out variables
nodes.rationale: Shaders exchange data with the programmable and configurable pipeline stages through global variables qualified in or out and given explicit layout locations.
nodes.norm_label: shader-pipeline communication: in and out variables

nodes.label: Built-in variable gl_Position
nodes.rationale: The vec4 a vertex shader must fill with the clipping coordinates of its vertex; other built-ins such as gl_VertexIndex and gl_InstanceIndex exist for the fixed pipeline stages.

nodes.label: Uniform variable blocks
nodes.rationale: Application-to-shader communication goes through uniforms, most often uniform blocks declared with a set and binding layout; each behaves like a C typedef struct whose fields are accessed with dot notation.

nodes.label: Vertex shader
nodes.rationale: The example vertex shader reads inPosition, multiplies it by the vpMat and worldMat taken from a uniform block to fill gl_Position, and forwards derived floats to the next stage.

nodes.label: Fragment shader
nodes.rationale: The example fragment shader receives the interpolated values, runs a bounded Mandelbrot-style loop driven by a time uniform, and writes the result into outColor.

nodes.label: E06 - Smooth surfaces and Advanced BRDF Techniques
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione - DEIB
nodes.rationale: Exercise deck covering how vertex normals encode smooth vs sharp solids, plus advanced BRDF models (Toon, Oren-Nayar, Ward, Cook-Torrance), material emission and ambient lighting.
nodes.norm_label: e06 - smooth surfaces and advanced brdf techniques

nodes.label: Vertex Normal Vector Encoding
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Whether a vertex position is stored once or duplicated depends on how many distinct normal directions the faces sharing it need: shared normals give smooth surfaces, differing normals give sharp edges.

nodes.label: Sphere Mesh Encoding (26 vertices, 48 triangles)
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A sphere of 4 rings and 8 slices needs only 26 vertices for 48 triangles because every vertex shares both position and normal direction across all its triangles.

nodes.label: Cube Mesh Encoding (24 vertices, 12 triangles)
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A cube needs 24 vertices for 12 triangles because each of the 8 corner positions must be repeated with three different normal vectors to keep the edges sharp.

nodes.label: Cylinder Mesh Encoding (34 vertices, 32 triangles)
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: An 8-sided prism cylinder mixes shared and duplicated normals, producing a sharp rounded border where cap normals point along y and side normals point radially outward.

nodes.label: Cone Tip Normal Workaround
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The tip of a cone admits no meaningful normal direction, so with Phong shading it is set to (0,0,0) to exclude it from interpolation, which yields correct shading everywhere except the (never displayed) limit point itself and lets the cone use a single top vertex.

nodes.label: Toon Shading
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Toon shading quantises the output colour into a few discrete values chosen by thresholds on the diffuse and specular dot products, producing a cartoon-like look.

nodes.label: 1D Texture Look-Up for Toon Ramps
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Multi-colour toon ramps with smooth transitions are implemented as 1D textures indexed by the cosine of the angle, which on modern GPUs is faster than program branches because texture look-up avoids divergence.

nodes.label: Oren-Nayar Diffuse Model
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A diffuse-only reflection model for very rough materials such as clay, dirt and cloth, parameterised by a colour mD and a roughness sigma, converging to Lambert when sigma is zero.

nodes.label: Retroreflection
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Rough materials tend to reflect light back toward the source, a phenomenon Lambert cannot reproduce and which motivates the Oren-Nayar model.

nodes.label: Oren-Nayar A and B Parameters
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Parameter A controls how closely the surface follows the Lambert principle while B controls the amount of retro-reflection; because the full formula is expensive, materials often give A directly and pre-compute the B term in a texture indexed by the two dot products.

nodes.label: Ward Anisotropic Specular Model
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A physically inspired specular model with two roughness parameters along the tangent and bi-tangent directions, so highlights stretch along surface grooves.

nodes.label: Anisotropic Materials
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Surfaces such as hair, CDs and brushed metal carry grooves that orient their specular highlights, so their reflection depends on direction within the surface plane.

nodes.label: Tangent and Bi-Tangent Vectors
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Two extra per-vertex vectors t and b, beside the normal, that specify the in-plane groove orientation needed for anisotropic reflection; how to encode or derive them is deferred to a later lesson.

nodes.label: Half-Vector
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The vector halfway between the light and viewer directions, introduced with the Blinn specular model and reused by both Ward and most Cook-Torrance D, F and G formulations.

nodes.label: Cook-Torrance Reflection Model
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A physically accurate BRDF whose specular term is the product of Distribution, Fresnel and Geometric terms, blended with a Lambert diffuse through a coefficient k; it is the building block for many advanced real-time techniques via pre-computed look-up textures.

nodes.label: Roughness Parameter (rho)
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A constant in [0,1] controlling how smooth the microscopic surface is, on which most of the D and G term definitions depend.

nodes.label: Distribution Term D
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The Cook-Torrance factor accounting for surface roughness, i.e. how microfacet normals are statistically distributed around the half-vector.

nodes.label: Blinn Distribution Version
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Adapts the Blinn specular model into the Cook-Torrance framework by replacing the specular power with the roughness parameter and adding a normalisation term.

nodes.label: Beckmann Distribution Version
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Uses the roughness to define the average microscopic slope of the surface, and can be simplified with trigonometric and dot-product identities.

nodes.label: GGX Distribution Version
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The GGX form of D has been shown to give the most realistic results while keeping complexity comparable to the Blinn version, which is why it is the usual PBR choice.

nodes.label: Fresnel Term F
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Approximated with the Schlick-style fifth-power expression around a parameter F0, it makes specular reflection grow as the light becomes almost parallel to the surface; the extended conductor version is out of scope.

nodes.label: Fresnel Principle
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Real objects reflect much more light at grazing angles, an effect Blinn and Phong cannot capture and which motivated more complex specular models.

nodes.label: Geometric Term G
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The Cook-Torrance factor accounting for microfacets shadowing and masking each other.

nodes.label: Microfacet Geometric Term Version
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: A parameter-free min-of-three formulation of G that depends only on the angles between normal, half-vector, light and viewer.

nodes.label: GGX Geometric Term Version
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Depends on roughness through a helper function gGGX evaluated once with the light direction and once with the viewer direction, whose product gives G.

nodes.label: Material Emission
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The emissive term mE adds light produced by the object itself, independent of the environment; it should only encode colours visible even in a dark scene and must not be abused to brighten objects that look too dark.

nodes.label: Ambient Lighting
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The simplest approximation of indirect illumination: a scene-wide constant RGB colour lA reflected by an ambient BRDF component fA that does not depend on the light direction, whose tint should match the scene (white and strong by day, bluish and dim at night).

nodes.label: Indirect Lighting
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: Illumination caused by light bouncing off other objects; ignoring it and using only direct sources produces very dark images.

nodes.label: Ambient Light Reflection Colour mA
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.rationale: The constant ambient BRDF, generally set equal to the diffuse colour mD but tunable for special lighting on particular objects.

nodes.label: Blinn 1977 - Model of Light Reflection for Computer Synthesized Pictures
nodes.source_file: Excercises/E06 - Smooth surfaces  Advanced BRDF Techniques.txt
nodes.author: J.F. Blinn
nodes.rationale: Source of the Cook-Torrance formulation used in the course, which differs from the version common in books and web sites because there the diffuse contribution is assumed constant.
nodes.norm_label: blinn 1977 - model of light reflection for computer synthesized pictures

nodes.label: E07 - Advanced Texturing
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione - DEIB
nodes.rationale: Exercise deck on normal maps and tangent space, the TBN frame, physically based rendering parameters and textures, and ambient plus hemispheric lighting.

nodes.label: Normal Maps
nodes.rationale: Textures that store a normal direction per internal point of a triangle, giving the appearance of a high-resolution mesh with few triangles because the normal is the most sensitive parameter of the illumination model.

nodes.label: Object Space Normal Maps
nodes.rationale: Encode x, y and z of the normal directly into RGB, which is simple and uses the full colour range but forbids repeating texture regions across the mesh and requires care when the object rotates.

nodes.label: Tangent Space Normal Maps
nodes.rationale: Express the normal in a local frame whose z-axis is the geometric normal, which makes the map reusable and rotation independent and gives it the characteristic cyan-magenta colour range.

nodes.label: Normal Map Colour Encoding and Decoding
nodes.rationale: Unit normal components in [-1,1] are linearly compressed to [0,1] when the map is authored and expanded back by the shader before use, so in simple cases the vertex normal attribute can be dropped entirely.
nodes.norm_label: normal map colour encoding and decoding

nodes.label: TBN Frame Matrix
nodes.rationale: The 3x3 matrix mat3(t, b, n) holding the tangent space axes, used to bring a tangent-space normal into world space regardless of how t and b were obtained.

nodes.label: Tangent and Bitangent Vectors (UV aligned)
nodes.rationale: The two secondary axes of tangent space, conventionally oriented along the U and V directions of the texture; the bitangent is usually derived by cross product so only normal and tangent need storing.

nodes.label: Tangent Storage vs On-the-Fly Computation Trade-off
nodes.rationale: Tangent and bitangent can be stored as extra vertex attributes, costing memory, or recomputed in the shaders, costing time; stored vectors must also follow the same transform as the normal and survive interpolation.
nodes.norm_label: tangent storage vs on-the-fly computation trade-off

nodes.label: Gram-Schmidt Re-orthogonalisation of the TBN
nodes.rationale: Interpolation across a triangle destroys both unit length and the right angle between normal and tangent, so a Gram-Schmidt step is applied per fragment to restore orthogonality before building the TBN.

nodes.label: Screen-Space Parameter Derivatives (dFdx / dFdy)
nodes.rationale: GLSL commands that approximate how an input variable changes along the horizontal and vertical screen directions, enabling per-fragment reconstruction of geometric quantities.

nodes.label: On-the-Fly Geometrical Normal in the Fragment Shader
nodes.rationale: The face normal can be rebuilt as normalize(cross(dFdx(fs_pos), dFdy(fs_pos))) even when no normal was stored with the geometry.
nodes.norm_label: on-the-fly geometrical normal in the fragment shader

nodes.label: On-the-Fly Tangent and Bitangent Computation
nodes.rationale: A multi-step fragment-shader recipe that derives the tangent from the screen-space derivatives of position and UV, re-orthogonalises it, gets the bitangent by cross product, and assembles the tbn matrix.

nodes.label: LearnOpenGL - Normal Mapping
nodes.rationale: External reference cited for the derivation of the tangent reconstruction formula.

nodes.label: PBR - Physically Based Rendering
nodes.rationale: An approximation of the rendering equation in which every material is described by just two normalised parameters, metalness and roughness, plus an albedo colour.

nodes.label: Metalness
nodes.rationale: A conceptually Boolean property (0 dielectric, 1 metallic) that engines nonetheless let artists set to intermediate values.

nodes.label: Metallic vs Dielectric Materials
nodes.rationale: Metals have almost no diffuse component and tint their specular reflections with the material colour, whereas dielectrics diffuse their own colour and reflect highlights in the colour of the incoming light.

nodes.label: Albedo
nodes.rationale: The main colour of a PBR object, usually supplied through a texture, and also used to derive F0 for metals.

nodes.label: PBR Implementation with Cook-Torrance GGX
nodes.rationale: PBR is realised as Cook-Torrance with GGX F, D and G, where the diffuse-specular mix k becomes one minus Fresnel and is further scaled by the complement of metalness so metals lose their diffuse contribution, and F0 is obtained empirically from metalness and albedo.

nodes.label: PBR Material Texture Set and Channel Packing
nodes.rationale: A PBR material ships up to six maps (albedo, normal, height, metalness, roughness, ambient occlusion) which artists pack into shared images -- height in the normal map alpha, and metalness, roughness and AO in the red, green and blue channels -- to cut the number of textures loaded.
nodes.norm_label: pbr material texture set and channel packing

nodes.label: PBR Material Libraries (freepbr.com)
nodes.rationale: Free online collections of ready-made PBR material texture sets, cited as an example of the format's popularity.

nodes.label: Hemispheric Lighting
nodes.rationale: An extension of ambient lighting with a sky colour lU, a ground colour lD and a direction d, blended by the cosine between the surface normal and d so that indirect light depends on how the surface is oriented.

nodes.label: E08 - Image Based Lighting
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione - DEIB
nodes.rationale: Exercise deck on encoding environment illumination in images: spherical harmonics, cube maps, skyboxes, environment maps, PBR combined with IBL through the split-sum approximation, and ambient occlusion.

nodes.label: Image Based Lighting
nodes.rationale: Generalises hemispheric lighting to an arbitrary function lA(x) returning the environment colour received from the direction of the surface normal, obtained from photographs or offline renders and encoded for real-time use.

nodes.label: Environment Filtering
nodes.rationale: The pre-processing step that turns a captured environment image into maps giving the total light received from each direction, so the rendering equation approximation stays the same and only the light function changes.

nodes.label: Cubic Mapping Encoding of lA(x)
nodes.rationale: One of the common ways to encode the ambient light function: interpolate values stored in a table addressed as a cube.

nodes.label: Spherical Harmonics
nodes.rationale: A spectral expansion writing the incoming colour as a sum of basis functions indexed by l and m, where truncating at l<=2 captures a wide range of illumination with only nine coefficients.

nodes.label: Six Direction Ambient Lighting
nodes.rationale: A custom ambient term invented for this course using six colours, one per signed axis direction, selected by the sign of the normal components and blended by their squares, which sum to one because the normal is unitary.

nodes.label: Cube Maps
nodes.rationale: Textures addressed by a 3D direction vector that encode the light incoming from every direction, the standard container for image based lighting data.

nodes.label: Skybox
nodes.rationale: The simplest use of a cube map: fill pixels covered by no primitive with the far-away environment, using only the rotation part of the camera matrix and forcing the projection so the cube sits as far as possible.

nodes.label: Perfect Fake Mirrors
nodes.rationale: Mirror reflections simulated by sampling the same skybox cube map along the reflected ray direction.

nodes.label: Environment Maps
nodes.rationale: A cube map read along -reflect(v,n) gives the environment colour in the reflected direction, scaled by an influence factor and added to the diffuse colour.

nodes.label: PBR combined with IBL
nodes.rationale: Pairing physically based materials with image based environment data gives realistic approximations of the rendering equation, with diffuse and specular parts approximated in two different ways.

nodes.label: IBL Diffuse Approximation
nodes.rationale: The diffuse part reduces to fetching the pre-filtered cube map in the direction of the normal and multiplying by the albedo.

nodes.label: Split-Sum Approximation
nodes.rationale: Splits the specular IBL integral into a prefiltered term depending on environment and roughness and a BRDF term depending mainly on the Cook-Torrance Fresnel component, both pre-computed as maps.

nodes.label: Prefiltered Specular Term
nodes.rationale: A family of look-up cube maps generated per roughness level and fetched along the reflected ray; rougher levels can be stored at lower resolution because the reflection is blurrier anyway.

nodes.label: BRDF Term (A and B Look-Up Texture)
nodes.rationale: A modification of the Fresnel term using coefficients A and B that are independent of the material and therefore can be read from the red and green channels of a single texture indexed by n.wr and roughness.
nodes.norm_label: brdf term (a and b look-up texture)

nodes.label: MipMap Levels as Filtered Environment Approximation
nodes.rationale: Instead of running a dedicated filtering tool, the MipMap chain generated on texture load can stand in for the roughness levels, with the pre-filtered diffuse resembling the last-but-one 2x2 level.
nodes.norm_label: mipmap levels as filtered environment approximation

nodes.label: cmftStudio Environment Filtering Tool
nodes.rationale: A dedicated tool that filters environment maps and produces the pre-filtered images required at render time.

nodes.label: Ambient Occlusion
nodes.rationale: A pre-computation of indirect light measuring how much sky each surface point can see; strictly it depends on position and scene changes, but the variation is small enough that it is baked into a texture shipped with modern materials.

nodes.label: E09 - Animation
nodes.author: Marco Gribaudo, Marco Domenico Buttiglione - DEIB
nodes.rationale: Exercise deck on 3D animation: key-frames and animation channels, Bezier interpolation, quaternion interpolation with nlerp and slerp, and animation baking and playback.

nodes.label: 3D Animation
nodes.rationale: The recording and reproduction of a 3D scene evolving in time, measured in frames per second.

nodes.label: Persistence of Vision
nodes.rationale: Showing at least 24 frames per second makes the eye perceive a continuous flow, the same principle cinema relies on.

nodes.label: Continuous Interpolation and Playback Resampling
nodes.rationale: Unlike cinema, display refresh is faster than the authoring rate and each frame takes a different time to render, so frames are interpolated into a continuous evolution and resampled at whatever instants the visualisation process needs.

nodes.label: Key-Frame Animation
nodes.rationale: A technique inherited from cartoon animation where artists draw story phases, extreme poses and breakdown poses and the in-between poses fill the rest; in 3D the in-betweens are generated automatically, saving memory and authoring time and making playback speed independent.

nodes.label: Animation Channels
nodes.rationale: Only parameters that actually change over time are stored as channels (a car x coordinate, a cannon pitch, a diffuse colour, a light direction), because storing every parameter of every object would be unaffordable.

nodes.label: Key-Frame Interpolation Continuity
nodes.rationale: Human vision is very sensitive to speed changes, so linearly interpolating key-frame values makes motion look blocky because the first derivative is discontinuous; techniques preserving velocity continuity are used instead.

nodes.label: Bezier Curves
nodes.rationale: A non-linear interpolation defined by N+1 control points, computed recursively from repeated linear interpolations, passing through the first point at alpha=0 and the last at alpha=1.

nodes.label: Linear Interpolation (lerp)
nodes.rationale: The elementary blend (1-alpha)a + alpha*b that all Bezier constructions and baked-animation playback are built from.

nodes.label: Bezier Polynomial Form
nodes.rationale: Factorising the control points out of the recursive definition yields a Bernstein polynomial expression, given explicitly for the second and third degree.

nodes.label: Third-Degree Bezier Curves for Animation
nodes.rationale: Cubic segments let each key-frame carry both a value and a first derivative through in and out tangents, so chained segments sharing endpoints give motion continuous in position and velocity.

nodes.label: Ease-In and Ease-Out
nodes.rationale: By moving the intermediate control points animators create discontinuities, straight lines and control how the motion accelerates in and decelerates out of a key-frame.

nodes.label: Bezier Segment Evaluation from Time
nodes.rationale: Each segment is stored as start and end frame plus four control values; at time t in seconds the segment covering t is found using the frame rate R, alpha is normalised inside it, and every coordinate is evaluated with a cubic Bezier.

nodes.label: Quaternions in 3D Animation
nodes.rationale: Rotations are converted from Euler angles to quaternions for interpolation and back to matrices for rendering, because quaternions avoid Gimbal lock, interpolate along a coherent path and have no modulo 360 issues.

nodes.label: Gimbal Lock
nodes.rationale: The degeneracy affecting Euler angle rotations that quaternions are immune to, the main reason animation pipelines interpolate in quaternion space.

nodes.label: nlerp (Normalized Linear Interpolation)
nodes.rationale: Interpolates the four quaternion components linearly and renormalises the result; simple and effective, but the rotation speed is not constant and care is needed not to travel the outer arc.

nodes.label: slerp (Spherical Linear Interpolation)
nodes.rationale: Interpolates on the sphere so the rotation speed stays constant when alpha encodes time, at the cost of transcendent function evaluations.

nodes.label: Bezier Curves for Rotation Animation
nodes.rationale: Because the Bezier construction is just nested interpolations, replacing lerp with slerp or nlerp extends Bezier curves to quaternions.

nodes.label: Animation Curves and Timeline Authoring
nodes.rationale: Authoring tools expose a frame-based timeline where the user inserts key-frames recording the current transform and then edits curve tangents to shape the interpolation.

nodes.label: Animation Baking
nodes.rationale: Key-frame curves are best for editing but are resampled at uniform time instants before shipping, so 3D applications can consume them with simple lookups.

nodes.label: Baked Animation Playback
nodes.rationale: At time t the application derives the frame index from the baked rate R and linearly interpolates the two neighbouring samples, using slerp or nlerp instead for rotations.

nodes.label: The Animator's Survival Kit (Richard Williams)
nodes.author: Richard Williams
nodes.rationale: Reference cited for the hierarchical key-frame drawing methodology inherited from the cartoon industry (Faber & Faber, 2nd edition, 2009).
